8 Reasons a Contractor Might Give You an Outrageously High Estimate

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high.
  • Industry observers note that if you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us.
  • In a recent development, I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

If you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high. A team of contractors weighs in with possible explanations.

Industry observers note that if you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us. In fact, it’s a pretty common occurrence. Sometimes, though, the quote is so high that you can feel your mouth forming words you shouldn’t be saying. As someone who has been on both sides of such interactions, I can say that contractors don’t like them any more than you do. They know you can shop around, and they need your business. So what’s the deal with ridiculously high quotes?

In a recent development, I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts. If a quote just made you hyperventilate, take a deep breath and check out some of the possible reasons why it’s so much higher than you expected.

“If an HVAC unit has a defective part that needs replacement, most of my clients will immediately ask how much the replacement part costs,” says HVAC technician Tamer Sayed. “I always tell the current market price and the misunderstanding often starts here. A few clients forget to take into account the labor and consultation fees. They assume they only had to pay for the replacement part.”.

The same thing can happen with plumbing and electrical jobs. The part needed to get things working again may be small and inexpensive, and it may only account for a small portion of the quote. Sometimes the labor quote seems excessive, and that’s usually because the client doesn’t understand what’s involved with the repair.

Recent findings suggest that jake Vincett, a builder from the UK, makes this observation: “A lot of the time, the customer is comparing quotes for different work, because the cheaper one has included a surface repair whereas the more expensive one has quoted for fixing the underlying problem…It’s common that the customer doesn’t know or consider the amount of work going into a project. A new driveway isn’t just laying tarmac – it’s digging out the old one, laying the sub base, etc.”.

Recent findings suggest that plumbing, electrical and HVAC expert Bob Cardwell adds: “It’s often not only one problem to fix but a bunch of small fixes. Even though it might be possible to fix the original problem without addressing the additional issues, an experienced and reliable technician will not ignore them, will try to fix them and will discuss them with the homeowner.”.

Industry observers note that failing to provide a quote that addresses underlying concerns and then delivering a sky-high bill at the end doesn’t just make the customer unhappy, claims HVAC and plumbing expert Ryan Osterkamp. “It can make them feel like we don’t know what we’re doing.”.

Osterkamp is used to hearing customers say: “I can go get that part for $X at Home Depot.” What they aren’t thinking about is the amount of training and expertise that made it possible for our technician to quickly and accurately diagnose the glitch, have the supplies they need in their truck and be able to do the repair same day. Sure, you may save money by going with the guy on Facebook that works out of an old, unlabeled truck, but if his work doesn’t hold up, will he fix it without giving you the runaround? Is he insured? Does he offer a warranty?”.

Tariffs, inflation and the economy in general are pushing prices up, and the dollar has lost a lot of its purchasing power for the average American. The same is true for contractors. “The fact of the matter is, we’re working harder now and making less,” says remodeling contractor Kevin Cullen. “In today’s economy, a lot of people are chasing the price to the bottom and shopping for the cheapest number. Unfortunately, they usually get what they pay for.”.

A contractor who knows problems might creep up, such as a rotten subfloor that needs replacement during a toilet repair, makes an effort to warn customers as part of the quote. Potential problems aren’t always obvious. “There are times,” says Nika Tveretinova, who operates an HVAC business in Sacramento, “when the actual fix isn’t that complicated, but it’s the access that makes things tough—especially with equipment installed in an attic or cramped quarters. Sometimes we also find an old installation that needs a safety or code correction before we can put everything back together.”.

In such situations, a higher-than-expected quote that you can reject is far better than a higher-than-expected bill you have to pay because the work is already completed.

According to recent reports, joshua Kurz founded NumeralQ, a home improvement pricing guide, and he cautions against comparing a bid you receive from a contractor to information you find online. “Owners often find an estimate online, and rather than waiting for a bid, they assume that number will be the actual cost. These estimates are helpful when determining a budget, but they are not interchangeable for actual bids. A 1,500 sq ft roof in one market will not necessarily cost the same in another market, and bids can even differ for neighboring houses.”.

Roberto Jimenez Mejias/Getty Images.

If you find a guy on Facebook who charges a low price to do a repair, there’s no guarantee that the repair will last or be up to code. When that person makes a mistake, a licensed contractor working on the same system at a later date might have to fix it, especially when inspectors are involved.

According to recent reports, “Over a 40-year career,” notes Cullen, “I’ve found many surprises: unsupported headers, no king or jack studs, undersized headers, poorly installed headers that aren’t flush and have gaps, termite damage, carpenter ant damage, water damage, mold. That’s not every job, but you never know when a homeowner bought a house in which a Rube Goldberg did the work on it.”.

Sometimes a house is in such poor condition that a small repair, such as stopping a plumbing leak, can turn into a major project that involves replacing pipes, walls or subfloors. Rather than simply declining the repair, some contractors will offer a ridiculously high quote to avoid falling into a sinkhole of extra work. If the customer accepts the quote, the contractor won’t lose money by taking the job. A customer who rejects a bid can keep shopping with no harm done.

Sources indicate that between 1997 and 2000, Hiland held various positions in the office of Governor Mike Huckabee. None required a JD. In a recent development, usually, law school graduates immediately take the bar exam. Perhaps Hiland was too busy serving as an aide to the governor to do so right away. Maybe he took it for the first time in February 2002, either two or three years after graduating from law school.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Not all electronic cords look the same.
  • Recent findings suggest that those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

It has been revealed that those little holes in electrical plug prongs have a purpose, but it isn't what most people think. Here's why they're still there.

Not all electronic cords look the same. Some have two prongs; others have three or even four. Some have prongs at weird angles, or are even designed for orange electrical outlets. Odds are most people have also seen electrical prongs with holes in them, but the reason for them isn’t common knowledge.

Recent findings suggest that those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them. Learn how the feature started, why some manufacturers still use them, what homeowners should know about plug safety, and more.

The holes originally helped keep plugs from slipping out of outlets. Some older outlets had small bumps inside that fit into the holes when someone plugged something in. That changed when Underwriters Laboratories began requiring outlets to hold plugs securely without those bumps.

“Most manufacturers stopped putting the detent nibs on the female contacts, as it made it much harder to meet the maximum force to withdraw and did nothing for the minimum requirement, as the gage had no holes,” according to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).

Basically, the bumps made plugs harder to remove, so manufacturers stopped using them. Today, outlets grip the prongs instead. If a plug starts slipping out, the outlet may need to be replaced. The holes aren’t a child safety feature, either. Tamper-resistant outlets use built-in shutters to keep children from sticking objects inside.

Industry observers note that “TRRs work like normal outlets,” according to the Electrical Safety Foundation International. “When you plug into a TRR for the first time, you may be able to feel the internal shutter system engaging. If excessive force is needed to insert a plug into a TRR, there’s a chance that the plug, not the receptacle, is damaged.”.

Manufacturers sometimes use the holes to hold the metal prongs in place while making plugs. They don’t help electricity flow through the plug, though. The holes can also hold small safety tags or locks on unplugged appliances. However, these shouldn’t replace proper safety equipment. OSHA also has rules for preventing equipment from accidentally starting during certain types of workplace maintenance.

The holes aren’t even required under American electrical plug standards. Manufacturers can make plugs without them, although NEMA has rules for their size and placement when included. They also have nothing to do with grounding. On a three-prong plug, the round prong handles that job. The two flat prongs work the same way whether they have holes or not.

Sources indicate that though in wintertime a window seat affords postcard-perfect views of snow-covered tree branches, it’s not necessarily the most comfortable perch on a cold day. During the chilly season, so much heat can escape through the panes of glass as well as through any cracks or gaps around the window frame that you’ll want to wrap up in a blanket, or at least put on a sweater, before you risk sitting so close to a window. The Energy Information Administration reports that the average home loses as much as a third of its energy as a result of poor window insulation. Luckily, there are several ways to mitigate this loss. Follow these best practices for how to insulate windows, and you can secure a warmer winter with just one weekend of work.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

It has been revealed that decades of exposure to the elements can wear away one of your main defenses against heat loss: exterior caulking. Once this begins to crumble, cracks can start to form around the window frame. If your windows are drafty, take swift action to replace the exterior caulking along the window frames before the weather takes a turn for the worse.

Sources indicate that check the weather before you begin the process. For successful application of caulking, you’ll want clear skies for 24 hours—no snow or rain—and, ideally, temperatures above 45 degrees Fahrenheit.

It has been revealed that use a putty knife to scrape window edges clean out the old caulking and peeling paint. Then, wipe the surface clean of any remnants with a damp rag. Let the surface dry for a few hours so the upcoming caulking will readily adhere. It’s best to start the project early in the day to allow enough dry time. You could also leave it to dry overnight.

Load your no-drip caulking gun with a cartridge of silicone exterior caulk and hold it at a 45-degree angle in order to get deep into the cracks around the window frame. Apply a solid, continuous bead of caulking between the frame and the siding, all the way around the window. Any caulk that oozes out of the crack should be pushed in gently with a putty knife.

Allow this to cure overnight to provide the best protection from wind and moisture.

Sources indicate that the sash, the part of the window that moves to open and close, is the area most homeowners zero in on when they’re trying to improve window insulation. While this area is vital, don’t neglect the glass itself or ignore other draft-curbing solutions. Take a multistep approach to insulating the inside of your windows by employing weatherstripping, window film, and energy-smart window treatments. Though we present this step-by-step approach as a process, you’ll still gain energy savings if you don’t complete every step.

Note: When you’re selecting replacement weatherstripping, closely consider the pros and cons of each material. As with many building materials, you get what you pay for in terms of lifespan. Felt, for example, is a common pick for its low price, but it can fail within only a few years. Adhesive-backed foam and tubular gasket stripping, on the other hand, are both cost-effective compression seals that work reliably and provide 3 to 5 years of protection from the cold.

It has been revealed that if your weatherstripping is worn or crumbling, it’s time to remove and replace it. Adhesive-backed stripping can simply be pulled up by hand. If the weatherstripping is attached with nails or screws, however, you must first remove the fasteners with a claw hammer or drill before you can lift it away. Once you’ve pulled the weatherstripping off, wipe down the window sash with a damp rag or paper towels and household cleaner. Allow it to dry thoroughly.

Industry observers note that measure your sash carefully, then cut the weatherstripping of your choice to length. Start as close as you can to the end of one side of the sash, peel off any adhesive backing, then carefully press the weatherstripping into place on the sash, making your way carefully to the other end.

“One insulating technique I love and have done many times requires the trim to be off (if, say, you’re installing a latest window or entry door): fill the voids between the door or window jamb and the rough framing with low-expanding foam insulation.”.

—Mark Clement, Contributing Writer.

Sources indicate that with the latest weatherstripping in place, you’ll want to double up your efforts with a window insulation kit. In addition to retaining up to 55 percent of your home’s heat in winter, this type of window covering will reflect heat and block UV rays from passing through uncovered windows, lowering indoor temperatures in summer and saving energy costs year-round. Before you proceed, check to see if your windows are still under warranty; the addition of window film may void the contract. If you’re in the clear, select the best quality insulating window film you can find for the job. Cheap versions can make the outdoors seem darker and even somewhat blurry. While that’s not a major issue for windows in some rooms, for more prominent windows, you may want to invest in higher-quality film that causes little to no loss of clarity and light.

Note: Cheaper methods that produce a similar insulating effect involve heat-and-shrink film or even bubble wrap, but these are often less attractive options that hamper or prevent the use of the windows, or hinder visibility. These inexpensive fixes, however, can be effective, easy to apply, and energy-efficient solutions for basement or attic windows.

Recent findings suggest that whichever method you choose, installation instructions vary from product to product. In general, start by washing the windowpanes so that no dust or lint gets trapped during application, then follow the manufacturer’s directions for installing the window film.

Best Home blackout curtains keep out up to 99% of light with triple-weave polyester construction and a layer of black yarn. Read the review.

According to recent reports, for one last defense against heat loss and drafts, consider hanging thermal curtains. For best insulating effects, install the curtain rod above and past each window on either side so the curtains fully cover the window frame. If it’s not appropriately installed, make adjustments to the rod’s position to maximize heat retention. While other window treatments like blinds or sheers offer some protection from drafts, a set of heavy curtains that you draw shut after dusk can cut heat loss by up to 17 percent.

Whether you ultimately decide to complete just one or all of these steps, you’ll still reap benefits. The more solutions you employ, however, the greater heat retention and energy savings you’ll see, and potentially not just in winter, but all year-round. If you’ve tried all these methods and still have poor window insulation, it might be time to replace your home’s windows.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production next year as Elon Musk shifts attention to its Cybercab. Here's what the change means.

Tesla Cybertrucks have dominated headlines even before they hit the road. But now it appears their time in the automotive world spotlight might be coming to an end. The tech giant’s CEO Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to make room for the Cybercab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

Learn why the firm is changing direction and what the news means for the Cybertruck.

Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images.

In a Nov. 6 post on X, Musk wrote, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”.

In a recent development, tesla began delivering Cybertrucks in late 2023, but sales haven’t lived up to expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates published by Cox Automotive, U.S. sales fell by nearly half in 2025. The truck has also faced criticism for its price, design, and quality concerns, as well as several safety recalls.

Industry observers note that current owners can continue driving their Cybertrucks, and existing warranty terms still apply. Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill also addressed concerns about future repairs. “Tesla will maintain spare parts and service will continue support,” he wrote on X on November 6. He didn’t specify how long that support would last.

It has been revealed that for anyone still waiting on a Cybertruck, the news is less encouraging. In a Nov. 9 post on X, Musk wrote, “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

Tesla hasn’t noted which customers will receive their trucks or how it plans to handle the remaining orders.

What Should You Do With Pumpkins After Halloween?

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife?
  • It has been revealed that before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips.
  • “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife? Experts explain the options.

It has been revealed that before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips. In the New World, they started carving pumpkins, which were readily available and far more dramatic. Since then, the Halloween tradition they established in the 19th century has only grown more popular and sees more and more pumpkins discarded every year.

In a recent development, how many? “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.

If you care about soil, wildlife and the environment in general, there really is a right way and a wrong way to dispose of pumpkins after Halloween. A gardening expert, a composting expert and a worm farmer explain the difference.

Industry observers note that definitely, yes. “There are many ways to compost a pumpkin,” indicates Click. “I chop mine up into smaller pieces and feed it to my indoor worm compost farm. You can compost all parts of a pumpkin as long as it is not treated with chemicals, has no paint (so, no painted pumpkins), no glitter, and no plastic/wax/metal candle residue. You can even compost moldy/gross pumpkins!”.

It’s crucial to chop up the pumpkin and not throw it on the compost pile whole, adds UK gardener David Denyer. “Pumpkins decompose slowly if left whole because of their thick rind and high water content. Because of this, adding them straight to your compost can throw off the balance, making the heap turn slimy or even anaerobic, which stops it from breaking down properly.”.

One option is to give them to animal rescues and local farmers to use as feed for pigs, chickens and livestock. Click loves this option because, as she claims, many farmers compost manure, which makes it a win-win situation. The pumpkin winds up providing nourishment in the soil for more pumpkins.

If you live in the city, worm farmer Scott Kent has another suggestion: “Take your leftover pumpkins is to a worm farm! Composting worms, like red wigglers, consume organic waste and create worm castings from it. Pumpkins, and most all other cucurbits for that matter, are among composting worms’ most favorite foods.”.

According to recent reports, for a quick way to recycle pumpkins after Halloween that you can do at home, cut the pumpkin into small chunks and bury them in your garden. “This works like a green manure,” says Denyer, “adding organic matter below the surface where it can decompose safely without attracting any pests or spreading disease.”.

This is generally a bad idea, say our experts. Click worries about attracting wildlife to areas in which they can be harmed, but beyond that, decomposing pumpkins are not the best source of nutrition. “The acidity and mold that develops as they rot can make hedgehogs, insects, and birds unwell,” says Denyer, who lives where hedgehogs are a thing.

Sources indicate that the danger to wildlife increases if the pumpkin contains toxic materials. If you wouldn’t feed, paint, glitter or candle wax to a pet, you shouldn’t feed it to wildlife.

According to recent reports, before carving a pumpkin, most people remove the seeds. Don’t throw them out. When you roast them, they make a delicious snack. After the seeds are gone, the rind makes a good (if temporary) planter for displaying your fall blooms on the porch. Just remember to line the inside to prevent dirt from spilling out from the face you carved.

According to recent reports, composting may be the best way to recycle a pumpkin rind, but if you’re okay with a less dramatic jack-o’-lantern, a smaller pumpkin like a Hokkaido or Baby-Bear can serve a double purpose. Unlike large carving pumpkins with thick, waxy skins, these smaller varieties have thin skins and a high sugar content that make them delicious in soup.

Don’t just toss  them in the garden, warns Denyer: “Pumpkins are high in water and sugars, which means they promptly break down into a thick, slimy layer that blocks air circulation and traps moisture around plant roots. This can then encourage fungal problems, like grey mold or powdery mildew, which can spread to nearby plants.”.

It’s important to check with the local waste management rules, because some communities don’t allow pumpkins in yard waste bins. If your community allows them, remove candle wax and other inorganic materials.

Recent findings suggest that painted pumpkins present a problem: They are organic, but because of the paint, you shouldn’t throw them in organic waste, and some communities prohibit organic materials in the general trash. In such cases, cutting up and burying your pumpkins after Halloween is probably the best solution.

Sources indicate that if you leave a whole pumpkin out in the field, it will start decomposing about eight or 12 weeks after it’s fully ripe. Once you cut a pumpkin into smaller pieces and throw them in a compost pile, the pieces will start to rot in five to 10 days.

Full decomposition depends on the moisture content of the air and soil, and on the temperature. It occurs faster when there’s lots of moisture and the air is warm.

Generally, no. Most paints contain toxic chemicals that can poison the compost and the soil on which you spread it. This isn’t necessarily true for all paints, including some water-soluble plant- or egg-based children’s paints, but if you don’t know where the paint came from, keep the painted pumpkin out of the compost.

A paint may be safe for kids, but that doesn’t mean it’s safe for composting. Crayola, a manufacturer of safe-to-use paints for children, recommends using them on pumpkins but warns that those pumpkins should not be consumed (meaning they should not go in the compost).

Yard Eyesores That Ruin Your Curb Appeal

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.
  • In a recent development, what makes a yard an eyesore?
  • In a recent development, the good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

In a recent development, what makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

In a recent development, the good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

According to recent reports, unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can promptly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland says. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”.

Industry observers note that vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can promptly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception concern if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes says.

Broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can quickly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty states. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”.

Fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be new to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker notes. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”.

Adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker says. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”.

While low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes says. But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

According to recent reports, A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes says. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

“There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty states. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the significant deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

Industry observers note that broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

While they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland notes. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

“A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland notes. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our newly introduced neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

Kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty claims. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.

Your riding lawnmower can do double duty this winter by adding a snow plow. Here’s what you need to know before adding a plow to your riding mower.

Snow is considered a “four-letter” word in our home. Living in the northeast, right in the middle of the so called “I-95” corridor, we usually average 20 inches of snow a year. Even with my trusted 26-inch two-stage snow blower and my newest gadget, an 18 volt snow shovel, clearing the driveway and sidewalk can promptly turn into a significant time consuming and dangerous job. If you already own a riding mower (different from a lawn or garden tractor), you may wonder if you can add a snow plow to turn it into a useful piece of year-round equipment.

The short answer is “yes, maybe,” said David Bodzioch, certified Small Engine and Automotive Technology Instructor. Snow (plow) blades are available for certain riding mowers. However, Bodzioch cautioned, “attaching a blade doesn’t necessarily make your mower ready to clean a snow-covered driveway.”.

Sources indicate that accessory compatibility, traction, mower size as well as the amount and type of snow you typically need to move will determine if you can, or should, add a plow blade to your riding lawnmower. Before investing in a plow, you need to understand what your mower can realistically handle. As well as determining what accessories you might need. Here’s what our experts have to say about turning a riding mower into a snow plow.

“Yes, many riding lawnmowers can be equipped with a front-mounted snow blade,” said certified Small Engine instructor Jeffrey Cesari. “Even if aftermarket compatible attachments are available, you should use the manufacturer’s approved attachments,” added Cesari. “Adding a plow blade on small tractors requires a set of rear wheel chains and a counterweight for balance,” added Cesari.

For example, John Deere sells a front blade package (as well as snow throwers) designed for specific riding lawnmowers. A John Deer 19 horsepower or better twin-cylinder engine units position the driver closer to the engine for better balance.

What Do You Need to Turn a Riding Lawnmower Into a Snow Plow?

It has been revealed that “At minimum, you’ll need a snow blade and direct-fit mounting hardware designed to fit your particular make and model mower,” remarked Bodzioch. Tire chains and weights should also be considered when operating snow-clearing equipment. According to Troy-Bilt, makers of outdoor power equipment, “Depending on the riding lawnmower mower and snow conditions, the mower will benefit from the added traction that chains and weights provide” when removing snow.

“It depends on whether your mower simply requires a blade, or the added cost of mounting hardware, weights and tire chains,” said Cesari. An add on blade can cost as little as $120 for 22 to 32 inch width universal riding mower plow kit, to over $1400 for a complete John Deere 46 inch front blade snow plow package that includes an adjustable three-position blade height and angle setting you can change from the driver’s seat. Look for heavy-gauge steel blades that are height-adjustable and have the ability to reposition the shave plate for longer life.

Sources indicate that the biggest advantage is getting year-round use from expensive equipment you already own. Plus, eliminating the need for another piece of snow-removal equipment that sits unused for nine or ten months out of the year.

In a recent development, “You’ll probably need to buy and install several accessories and that can be expensive,” remarked Bodzioch. You should also check how difficult it is swapping out the snow blade and grass cutting mower deck. He added that “you also want check if your mower and blade combination are right for your type [concrete, blacktop, etc.] driveway.”.

Yes, it can be, and should be, as long as your mower is approved for the attachment, is well-maintained and in good working condition. Following the manufacturer’s operating, maintenance guides and safety instructions is mandatory for safe and efficient operation; the same as when using any other piece of outdoor power equipment.

Bodzioch said, “Proper traction is especially vital when driving on ice and snow, or on snow-covered grass or soil.” But Cesari also notes that “you need to be aware of frame structure and that adding a snow plow can cause frame damage, transmission wear and belt fatigue on small home riding mowers.” Cesari said plowing up to five inches should be safe. Always be cautious and use common sense if your mower is struggling while removing any amount of snow.

Sources indicate that it depends. It may only make sense if you already own a compatible mower. However, having room and space to safely store the blade should be a real consideration. Cesari added, “Converting your mower to a plow may require buying expensive attachments or accessories. Consider a standalone snow blower or a lawn/garden tractor if it’s difficult swap out the mower deck and plow.” If you regularly deal with challenging snow conditions, a dedicated snow-removal machine may be the better investment.

Industry observers note that it depends on how you use the word. While “riding mower” and “lawn tractor” are often interchangeable, there are key differences between the two pieces of equipment. A riding mower typically means any mower you sit on, including a lawn tractor or zero-turn mower. Nevertheless, a lawn/garden tractor will generally be more expensive and have a larger, sturdier frame. Lawn/garden tractors are designed and built to accept manufacturers’ compatible direct-fit attachments and accessories.

Everyone recognizes an emergency siren. Or do they?

Industry observers note that officers can choose different tones to make their vehicles easier to notice on busy streets or open roads. Some departments also use certain sounds for special warnings. With electronic siren systems offering several options, drivers might hear multiple tones during a single emergency response.

Learn what the common sounds mean, why officers switch between them, whether different tones signal different emergencies, and how drivers should react.

Different police siren sounds serve different purposes, but they don’t necessarily indicate specific emergencies. Officers often switch tones based on traffic conditions or to get drivers’ attention. A faster siren doesn’t always mean a more serious emergency.

The most common police siren sounds include:.

Modern police vehicles typically use electronic sirens that allow officers to switch between these sounds. Older mechanical sirens use a spinning mechanism to produce a traditional wail.

Industry observers note that officers also adjust their sirens based on traffic conditions. Faster tones can help get drivers’ attention in heavy traffic, while a slower wail may work on quieter roads. Departments set their own policies for siren use, so there isn’t one standard sound for daytime or nighttime driving.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of the siren sound, drivers should respond the same way when an emergency vehicle approaches. Drivers should check their mirrors, signal, and safely pull toward the right side of the road to let the police vehicle pass. They should avoid sudden braking or stopping in an intersection.

Sources indicate that anyone already in an intersection should continue through before pulling over. Drivers waiting at a red light shouldn’t enter the intersection unless an officer directs them to do so. After the police vehicle passes, drivers should check for other emergency vehicles before returning to traffic. Specific rules may vary by state.

In a recent development, before learning how to clean windows with vinegar, you’ll first want to gather the materials for this DIY glass cleaner. You’ll need distilled white vinegar (or lemon juice) and dish soap—a fragrant essential oil is nice to add, but not necessary.

Recent findings suggest that in this recipe, as with so many other nontoxic homemade cleaners, white vinegar plays a key role. Its acidity cuts through dirt and grease, an attribute that well equips the window cleaner to remove stuck-on debris and streaks.

If you’ve washed your windows for years with a commercial cleaner such as Formula 409 or even Windex, it’s likely that the glass sports a subtle, waxy film. That residue comes off easily with ordinary dish detergent, another ingredient contributing to the efficacy of homemade window cleaner.

In a spray bottle, combine ¼ cup of white vinegar with ½ teaspoon of liquid dish soap. Dilute the solution with 2 cups of water, then shake the bottle vigorously to mix the components. Industry observers note that this window-cleaning recipe works like a dream, but what do the individual components contribute to the mix? We’ll break it down for you.

Like white vinegar, the acid in lemon juice can effectively break down grime on windows and other glass surfaces. Citric acid in lemon juice is technically a bit stronger than vinegar’s acetic acid, though both are about equally effective when it comes to cleaning around the house.

Recent findings suggest that several ingredients make up most liquid dish soaps on the market, but one ingredient in particular, sodium lauryl sulfate, gives dish soaps their impressive grease-busting abilities. The component bonds with oily particles and lifts them off of surfaces, which allows for easy removal when used with water.

Using natural ingredients is eco-friendly and safer for your skin and lungs compared to the chemicals found in many commercial cleaners, but there are still a few safety considerations to be aware of when making your own window cleaner. Natural ingredients such as white vinegar, lemon juice, and essential oils are effective in homemade glass cleaners, but they do not replace true sanitizers that are proven to kill 99.9 percent of disease-causing pathogens.

The most crucial thing to remember when making window cleaner (or any other homemade cleaning solutions) is never to mix vinegar with chlorine bleach. When sodium hypochlorite, the basic chemical compound in bleach, mixes with the acetic acid found in vinegar, it gives off toxic chlorine gas. Chlorine gas can burn skin, cause shortness of breath, and can even be fatal with long-term exposure.

Natural glass cleaners that do not contain ammonia, such as the homemade window cleaner recipe above, don’t leave behind residue or streaks when wiped away using a clean microfiber cloth.

The best window cleaning solution is safe, natural, and effective. Following this recipe for a natural window cleaner can help you achieve all of these goals and leave you with clear, clean, and streak-free windows. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some excerpts from the long opinion by Judge Thomas Thrash (N.D. Ga.) yesterday in Winer v. Mohammad:.

Industry observers note that this action arises out of alleged defamatory statements that Defendant Umaymah Mohammad, a student at the Emory University School of Medicine, made about Plaintiff Joshua Winer, a physician and professor at Emory. Mohammad, who is Palestinian, sent an email to the entire School of Medicine student and faculty body on January 17, 2024, in which the Plaintiff alleges she "praised terrorism against Israel, expressed her hatred towards Israel and the United States, and stated that Israel, the United States, and Emory are perpetrating a genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.".

It has been revealed that nearly two months later, in March 2024, the Plaintiff published an op-ed piece in an Israeli news publication sharing his decision to travel to Israel to volunteer as a physician in the Israeli Defense Force ("IDF") following the October 7th Hamas attack on Israel. The Plaintiff identifies as Jewish and maintains dual American and Israeli citizenship. He is a surgical oncologist at Emory Winship Cancer Institute, a professor in the Department of Surgery, Division of Surgical Oncology at the School of Medicine, and serves as the School of Medicine Surgical Clerkship Director.

In a recent development, in April 2024, Mohammad participated in an interview for a news organization called Democracy Now!. In the interview, Mohammad was asked about the email she sent and was asked to explain the importance of the matter to her. As part of her response, Mohammad referenced Winer by stating that.

Sources indicate that one of the professors of medicine we have at Emory recently went to serve as a volunteer medic in the Israeli Offense Force [sic] and recently came back. This man participated in aiding and abetting a genocide, in aiding and abetting the destruction of the healthcare system in Gaza and the murder of over 400 healthcare workers, and is now back at Emory so-called teaching medical students and residents how to take care of patients.

Mohammad was ultimately suspended from the School of Medicine for one year based on her comments in the Democracy Now! interview. In November 2024, Mohammad participated in a podcast hosted by the International Union of Scientists in which she made similar statements about the Plaintiff. In January 2025, she made more statements about the Plaintiff's IDF service in the online publication Mondoweiss. In the Mondoweiss piece, Mohammad claimed that the Plaintiff "believe[d] in the legitimacy of apartheid, and that some human lives are not as key as others.".

At the end of the piece, she provided a link to a social media post by Defendants National Students for Justice in Palestine ("NSJP") and Doctors Against Genocide ("DAG"), which ultimately led to a campaign on the website of Action Network that "contained additional false statements about Plaintiff and identified him by name." NSJP and DAG also published posts on Instagram regarding the Action Network campaign, which directly quoted Mohammad's Democracy Now! interview. These Defendants made a second Instagram post a few weeks later. The Plaintiff alleges that Defendant WESPAC is NSJP's fiscal sponsor and, therefore, "knowingly funded and facilitated NSJP's coordinated efforts to vilify Plaintiff and pressure Emory to discipline [him].".

In February 2025, Defendant CAIR Georgia held a press conference on the subject of Mohammad's suspension, during which she made the following statement:.

[Emory] disciplined me for exposing Emory's complicity in the destruction of Gaza in an interview where I mentioned an unnamed physician who served in the military, actively engaged in the genocidal campaign against the Palestinian people, my people … I cannot learn from a physician who might have fired one of the 355 bullets that landed in 6 year old Hind Rajab's body. Or who might have helped make the decision to bomb one of the hospitals in Gaza. Or who might have celebrated the murder of our communities on the rubble still wet with Palestinian blood. A doctor who cannot see Palestinians as human beings will return to Atlanta to offer the same disposability to black and brown patients at home.

Industry observers note that CAIR Georgia, along with CAIR Foundation Inc. ("CAIR Foundation"), also issued a press release with a link to Mohammad's Democracy Now! interview and rebroadcasted this speech on its Instagram account on February 11, 2025. In this post, (the "IG Post"), CAIR Georgia also replied to comments by providing a link to a previously circulated email template and phone script that identified the Plaintiff by name and called for Emory to investigate him and/or terminate his employment.

Industry observers note that mohammad's statements were later broadcasted and published by television stations and news outlets. Defendant Ibrahim Jouja was the President of Emory SJP when it shared NSJP and DAG's posts on the Emory SJP Instagram account, and also made or collaborated on similar posts sharing the Democracy Now! interview and identifying the Plaintiff "as a physician with military combat experience against Palestinians." Defendant Rupa Marya works with Mohammad as a cofounder of DAG and, the Plaintiff alleges, she has "frequently identified Plaintiff by name and used her social media platforms to spread harmful and reputationally damaging statements about him," including blaming him for the termination of a Palestinian professor at Emory School of Medicine and accusing him of participating in a genocide….

The court allowed plaintiff's federal claim for conspiracy to interfere with civil rights (42 U.S.C. § 1985) to go forward:.

Section 1985(3) "created a cause of action against private individuals who, among other things, undertake conspiracies for the purpose of depriving, either directly or indirectly, any person or class of persons of the equal protection of the laws, or of equal privileges and immunities under the laws." "That § 1985(3) reaches private action does not, however, mean that it was intended to apply to all tortious, conspiratorial interferences with the rights of others." ….

It has been revealed that the Plaintiff hinges [the remaining part of] his § 1985(3) claim on the alleged violations of his rights under … Title VI. The Eleventh Circuit does not appear to have addressed whether a violation of Title VI is enforceable against a private conspirator under § 1985(3), so for the reasons the Court expressed in its prior orders, the Court presumes that it is. To state a claim under § 1985(3), a plaintiff must establish that the defendant has.

(1) conspired or gone in disguise on the highway or on the premises of another, (2) for the purpose of depriving, either directly or indirectly, any person or class of persons of the equal protection of the laws, or of equal privileges and immunities under the laws, (3) taken or caused an action to be taken in furtherance of the conspiracy's object, and (4) injured an individual's person or property or deprived her of exercising any right or privilege of a United States citizen.

Title VI provides that no one shall "be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance" on the ground of his "race, color, or national origin." To state a claim under § 2000d, a plaintiff must only allege that the defendant receives federal funds, that it discriminated against the plaintiff on the basis of race, color, or national origin, and that it did so in the course of a federally funded program….

[Plaintiff asserts] a § 1985(3) claim based on a conspiracy to induce Emory to violate his Title VI rights. And for purposes of a motion to a dismiss, he has stated such a claim as to the CAIR Foundation theory. The Plaintiff alleges that CAIR Foundation receives federal funding, making § 2000d enforceable against it. More specifically, he alleges that CAIR Foundation received federal funding, that it conspired with the other defendants, including Mohammad and Jouja, to subject him to discrimination based on his race and national origin by posting the IG Posts at glitch, which he alleges were defamatory and filled with false accusations, and that this discrimination was carried out "in the administration of CAIR Foundation's program or activities receiving Federal financial assistance." The Plaintiff also identifies the specific actions he alleges the Defendants took in furtherance of the conspiracy, including the statements Mohammad made that Jouja is allegedly responsible for as president of Emory SJP. At this early stage, these allegations satisfy the elements of a § 1985(3) claim predicated on a Title VI violation.

Whether this claim can withstand summary judgment is a question for another day. Accordingly, the Defendants' Motion to Dismiss is denied as to this argument.

In the process, the court also held that plaintiff had adequately alleged the "protected class" element of § 1985(3), by alleging that he was targeted for his national origin:.

The Defendants next argue that the Plaintiff unfairly conflates anti-Zionism with antisemitism in order to "place an entire area of First Amendment-protected political, legal and ethical discussion off limits." … The Defendants essentially argue that because Zionism is (in their view) solely a political philosophy, the Plaintiff has actually alleged that their actions were not truly motivated by his Jewish identity but instead by their opposition to Zionism and serving in the IDF. But taking that view would require the Court to construe the Plaintiff's allegations narrowly and in their favor, which it cannot do at this stage.

What the Plaintiff actually alleges, if construed in his favor—and what the Court must accept as true at this stage—is that his military service resulted from a "sense of duty to serve the Jewish homeland, which is integral to his racial identity as a Jew" ["racial" is here used in the historical sense that included what we would now call "ethnicity," consistent with the Court's caselaw on § 1985 and related statutes -EV] and that his association with Zionism is also "an integral part of Jewish identity for a very significant number of Jews." In essence, the Plaintiff alleges that his military service and association with Zionism are markers of his own personal Jewish identity, and that his Jewish heritage as an Israeli national is a protected class.

Critical to this interpretation is the Plaintiff's allegations that his IDF service was tied to the duty he felt based on his nationality and the significance of Zionism in Jewish culture. These allegations suffice at this stage to demonstrate that a discriminatory animus based on a protected class—the Plaintiff's national origin—motivated the Defendants' actions, not mere political differences.

And the court concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that defendants' speech fell within the First Amendment exception for defamation. It concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that he wasn't a limited purpose public figure, despite his op-ed. And the court concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that the statements about him contained false factual assertions:.

According to recent reports, plaintiff asserts that parts of Mohammad's statement in the Democracy Now! interview are demonstrably false, including her statements that the Plaintiff "aid[ed and abett[ed] a genocide" and "aid[ed] and abett[ed] the destruction of the healthcare system in Gaza." Regardless of whether these statements express political opinion, the statements could reasonably "imply defamatory facts about the plaintiff that are capable of being proved false" when the facts are construed in the Plaintiff's favor[.] This is because Mohammad's statements—that the Plaintiff alleges Jouja is responsible for reposting as president of Emory SJP, along with supportive commentary—imply that the Plaintiff actively participated in combat operations during his service in the IDF, but the Plaintiff pled that he served.

In a recent development, solely in his capacity as a physician, providing medical care to wounded soldiers. His involvement in combat was limited to situations in which his unit came under direct attack … Mohammad had no factual basis to claim that Plaintiff participated in or approved the bombing of hospitals in Gaza [or] celebrated the killing of Palestinians.

Recent findings suggest that the Court agrees with the Defendants' position that characterizing the Israel-Hamas war as a genocide is likely an inactionable opinion because it reflects a "subjective assessment, as to which reasonable minds could differ, [and which] cannot be proved false." But the statements at issue here go further and allege personal combat participation in the alleged genocide—a fact which the Plaintiff could prove at a later stage is false. At this stage, his allegations about his role are enough to satisfy the "false and defamatory statement" element of his defamation per se claim and the falsity element of his false light claim.

The same is true of part of Mohammad's statement during the press conference, in which she stated that.

[h]aving a physician faculty member who participated in a military convicted of committing genocide against Palestinians makes me feel unsafe. It makes black and brown medical students feel unsafe. It makes black and brown and indigenous patients feel unsafe. I cannot learn from a physician who might have fired one of the 355 bullets that landed in 6 year old Hind Rajab's body. Or who might have helped make the decision to bomb one of the hospitals in Gaza … a doctor who cannot see Palestinians as human beings will return to Atlanta to offer the same disposability to black and brown patients at home.

It has been revealed that there are parts of the statement that express Mohammad's opinion, such as the part that the Plaintiff's military service makes her, and "black and brown medical students," feel unsafe. This is a subjective assessment that cannot be proved false, so this part of the statement is not actionable. But the part of the statement that suggests the Plaintiff might have been involved in combat decisions or actions and accuses him of not "see[ing] Palestinians as human beings" and offering "the same disposability to black and brown patients" at Emory certainly implies that the Plaintiff engaged in combat operations while serving in the IDF and that patients of certain races are therefore not safe in his care.

The same is true of the statement in Emory SJP's March 28, 2025 collaborative IG Post that described the Plaintiff as "a physician with military combat experience against Palestinians." The Plaintiff has alleged counter-facts that, if accepted as true, prove these portions of the statements false, so the Plaintiff states a claim as to these portions of the press conference statement and the March 28 Emory SJP IG Post.

In a recent development, for these reasons, the Court will dismiss the portion of the Plaintiff's defamation and false light claims predicated on the opinion portions of the statements identified above. The Court will deny the Defendants' Motion to Dismiss as to the remainder of their First Amendment and opinion-based arguments….

If the outlets in a room aren’t where you need them and you’ve got extension cords running amok, adding an outlet can eliminate those trip hazards and make everyday living a bit easier. Or maybe you need a fresh outlet in a bathroom, laundry room, or doggy wash station in your mudroom, which means you’ll need to install a ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlet, required for any outlet within 6 feet of a water source. The good news is, wiring an outlet, whether standard or GFCI, is a project that you can do yourself, but you must take proper safety precautions.

It has been revealed that however, if an outlet’s cover has melted, if the outlet has been smoking, or if there’s a burning smell, there’s likely a bigger problem than just the outlet. In these instances, it’s best to consult with a licensed electrician before you attempt to rewire it.

Read through these steps for how to wire an outlet before you get started.

Sources indicate that while a capable homeowner can wire an outlet, it’s not a job for a reluctant or unsure DIYer. Start by assessing your comfort level, and call in a pro if you have doubts.

In many instances, you can wire an outlet from another outlet. In fact, if there’s an existing outlet in a room on the opposite side of the wall from where you’d like to add an outlet, the job can be pretty simple. In this situation, you can usually cut a new opening, install an electrical box, and add a new outlet without having to snake wires through studs. Use a stud finder to locate the studs on either side of the existing outlet and make sure to situate the new outlet within the same stud bay.

Recent findings suggest that if you simply want more outlets in one location, it’s possible to replace an existing duplex outlet, which takes just two plugs, with a quad receptacle, which takes four. This can be helpful in a workshop or even in kitchens and bathrooms where two outlets just won’t cut it.

In either case, it’s important that there’s enough capacity on the circuit to accommodate the additional draw. For 15-amp circuits, the maximum is usually eight outlets or lights. Any more receptacles than that might draw too much current for the breaker.

Old-fashioned two-prong outlet connections aren’t grounded, which makes them dangerous in the event of an electrical fault. Without an electrician, it’s safe to convert a two-prong to a three-prong outlet only if the electrical box housing the outlet is metal and the cable feeding the box is armored. If these conditions are met, the box provides ground-fault protection (even though the outlet does not).

Sources indicate that how can you tell, without opening the wall, if the electrical box meets the criteria? Simple: Use a voltage tester. Insert one prong into the outlet’s shorter slot (the “hot slot”), then touch the other prong to the screw securing the faceplate. If the tester lights up, the electrical box is grounded, and you can go ahead and convert the two-prong to a three-prong. If your electrical box isn’t grounded, you can still convert to a three-prong, but the replacement must be a GFCI (the type of outlet with a red button on its front).

Over time, electrical outlets can start to look dingy or dirty, or the plastic can crack and make the outlet dangerous to use. To keep power flowing where you need it, it’s crucial to learn how to replace an electrical outlet safely and efficiently.

4-in-1 screwdriverVoltage testerOutlet.

In a recent development, before you go any further, it’s imperative that you cut power to the outlet you are replacing. At your home’s electrical panel, toggle off the switch associated with the circuit that sends electricity to the outlet in question.

Sources indicate that after you shut off the power to the outlet, use a voltage tester to double-check that it’s really off. Insert the tester’s probes into the top two slots on the outlet. If the tester lights up, you toggled the wrong switch on the electrical panel and you’ll have to try again. Continue by trial and error until you are certain the outlet is no longer receiving electricity. (When you’re done, relabel the circuits in the panel so you know which is which.).

Don’t have a voltage tester? You can use a lamp instead, so long as you know the lamp works. Plug the lamp into the outlet, and if it doesn’t turn on, it’s safe to proceed. This method is inherently riskier, so use it only as a last resort.

After you confirm that the power is off to the outlet, stick a piece of black electrical tape across the breaker so no one can flip it back on while you are working.

It has been revealed that the Fluke 1AC II has a flashing red  indicator to show that it’s working. A loud, audible beep sounds when it detects power. Read the review.

In a recent development, most faceplates have a single screw in the middle. Remove that screw, and the plate should come off easily. Next, unscrew the mounting screws that secure the outlet to the electrical box. Finally, gently pull the outlet away from the receptacle.

Sources indicate that you can now see three wires extending from the wall to the outlet. If the wires are attached to screws on the outlet, loosen those screws to free the wires. If the wires are snaked into holes in the back of the outlet, press the release slot and pull the wires out, assuming they don’t come out on their own. Put aside the old outlet.

Recent findings suggest that you’re now ready to wire in the replacement. First, connect the neutral wire (white) to the silver screw on the side of the outlet. Make sure to orient the hooked end of the wire so that its curve goes clockwise, the same direction in which you will tighten the screw.

Connect the ground wire to the green screw, using the technique described above.

Connect the hot wire (black) to the gold screw, the last one remaining on the outlet casing.

Carefully maneuver the wires back into the electrical box, then screw the outlet to the box using the mounting screws at the top and bottom. Finally, position the faceplate over the outlet and screw it back on.

Go back to the electrical panel and restore power to the outlet that you’ve finished replacing. Check the outlet installation by testing the device with a voltage tester or a lamp.

In a recent development, sometimes a simple replacement isn’t enough—you absolutely need another outlet. Maybe you want to accommodate a new appliance or entertainment device, or you’re setting up a workshop. You can frequently solve this problem by wiring a new outlet from an existing outlet on the other side of the wall from the desired location of the new outlet. This project is a bit more involved, but a safety-minded DIYer can take it on.

Note: Be sure you’re using an “old work,” “rework,” or “remodeling” electrical box for the fresh outlet. These boxes have tabs that squeeze the box against the back of the drywall to hold it in place.

4-in-1 screwdriverVoltage testerNeedle-nose pliersLineman pliersWire strippersDrywall sawElectrical cableOutletRemodeling box (also known as an old work box)Wire connectorsWire running kit (optional).

Be sure to shut off the power to the existing outlet before doing anything else. Check the outlet for power with the voltage tester, and then go to the electrical panel to shut off the corresponding breaker.

Recent findings suggest that head back to the outlet and use a voltage tester to ensure that the power is off. Once you confirm that the power is off, it’s a good idea to place a piece of black electrical tape across the breaker to prevent anyone from carelessly flipping it back on.

Industry observers note that place the electrical box face-first against the drywall where you plan to install it. Trace along the box’s edges with a pencil, and then cut along the marks with a drywall saw. Sometimes it’s easier if you score the drywall with a utility knife first.

Sources indicate that head back to the existing outlet. If it’s been some time since you shut the breaker, test the outlet again to make sure it’s still off. Next, remove the faceplate and remove the screws holding the outlet in the box. Carefully pull the outlet out and let it hang to one side, providing access to the back of the box.

Push the newly introduced wire through an opening in the back of the box, feeding enough wire into the wall to reach the new outlet opening plus 1 foot. This can be challenging, so be patient and use pliers to pull the tab open if necessary. On this same side, cut the new wire approximately 10 inches from the box. Carefully strip back the plastic sheathing, leaving approximately 1 inch of sheathing in the box.

It has been revealed that use the screwdriver to loosen the screws holding the existing wires onto the outlet and straighten the hooks with needle-nose pliers. Use wire strippers to remove approximately ⅝ inch of sheathing from the hot (black) wire and neutral (white) wire.

Recent findings suggest that still working with the existing outlet, cut a 6- to 7-inch length from the spool of electrical cable. Remove the white, black, and ground wires from within the sheathing, and strip the ends back approximately ⅝ inch. This wire is called a pigtail.

Use the lineman pliers to twist the ends of the existing wire, the upcoming wire, and one end of the pigtail into a clockwise twist. Do this in three sets: all black wires, all white wires, and all ground wires. Cap each twist with a wire connector.

According to recent reports, use the needle-nose pliers to bend the wires at the other end of the pigtail into a J-shape and hook them onto the outlet. White (neutral) goes to silver, black (hot) goes to gold, and ground goes to green. Be sure that the hooks are running clockwise before tightening the screws.

Industry observers note that head to the other side of the wall to the space you’ve cut out for the fresh outlet. If the new wire isn’t easy to find, use a fishhook or tape from a wire running kit to fish it out from the wall. Pull the electric outlet wiring through the new opening, and feed the end into the new remodeling box.

Fit the box into the opening and turn the screws attached to the tabs clockwise until the box is secure. You should have about 10 inches of upcoming wire coming through the box. Strip the plastic sheathing back to expose the hot, neutral, and ground wires, leaving approximately 1 inch of sheathed cable inside the box.

It has been revealed that use the wire stripper to strip the sheathing from the ends of the hot, neutral, and ground wires, exposing approximately ⅝ inch of bare wire. Use the needle-nose pliers to bend the ends of the wires into hooks, and slip them over the screws on the new outlet. Remember to follow typical receptacle wiring techniques: Connect the white wire to the silver screw, the black wire to the gold screw, and the bare copper wire to the ground screw. Finally, bend the wires so they will fold nicely as you attach the outlet to the box.

It has been revealed that tighten the screws at the top and bottom of the outlet until it is snug in the box. Put the faceplate on the outlet and tighten the screw. Flip the breaker back on and test the outlet.

Learning how to wire an electrical outlet isn’t overwhelmingly difficult, and it’s a skill that some DIYers will use time and time again. With a little bit of background and proper safety techniques, adding an outlet for a TV or a latest tool or appliance can be a breeze. Just remember to work safely, test and retest electrical outlets before you start, and follow the instructions above for a reliable and safe electrical outlet installation.

Industry observers note that there are many types of electrical wires, and to explain them all would require an electrical engineering textbook. The most common residential wiring, including standard electrical outlet wiring colors, involves three types.

You absolutely can wire a light switch to an outlet, and there are several ways to do so. The switch can either be installed between the source of the power (typically the panel) and the outlet, or on a loop after the outlet.

To install it in-line, simply run the wire through an electrical box, connect the hot wire to the switch so it can interrupt the flow of power, and then continue the hot wire out to the outlet and wire as normal.

It has been revealed that to install the light switch after the device, connect the neutral wire in the box as usual, then run a length of wire from the outlet to the switch. Connect one end of the wire to the existing hot wire in the box using wire connectors. Next, connect the black wire from this length to one side of the switch, and connect the white wire to the other side. Finally, head back to the outlet and connect the white wire to the gold screw and wrap black electrical tape around the wire to indicate that it is now the hot lead coming from a switch.

The easiest way to fix an outlet that does not have a proper ground wire is to replace it with a GFCI outlet. These devices detect ground faults and interrupt the circuit right away. Install a GFCI in place of the first power outlet in the run to offer grounding protection.

Of course, contact a local electrical inspector to ensure this meets local codes.

Before or After the Snow? Here’s the Right Time to Salt Your Driveway This Winter

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.
  • It has been revealed that the Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months.
  • Salting before a massive storm with heavy snow and ice accumulation is a good idea, but timing matters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.

It has been revealed that the Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months. Icy sidewalks, stairs and driveways are largely to blame for this seasonal uptick. Icy driveways are not only dangerous to walk on but also make driving and parking difficult. Ice melt salt is one of the best ways to keep driveways clear, but how should you best use it? Should you apply it before or after a storm — or both? Two industry experts weigh in on the best way to salt your driveway for optimal results this winter.

It depends. Salting before a massive storm with heavy snow and ice accumulation is a good idea, but timing matters.

Industry observers note that initiative to apply salt several hours before a storm hits for best results. It creates a salty coating that prevents the initial snowfall from bonding with the driveway surface. Pre-salting reduces total snow accumulation and makes snow removal easier once the storm is over. Avoid doing it too far in advance, or if rain is in the forecast, as the salt can be washed or blown away before the snow arrives. It’s not necessary to salt before a light snowfall of less than six inches.

Recent findings suggest that it’s always a good idea to salt after it snows, but don’t rely on it to replace snow removal efforts. First remove as much snow as possible with a shovel or snowblower, then use salt to clear away any remaining slush and snow.

Recent findings suggest that the best time to salt is immediately after snow removal, before cold nighttime temperatures set in. “When applied before the temperatures drop, salt prevents ice from forming and ensures the snow does not freeze solid to the ground,” Angelika Klimorowski, a winter maintenance specialist at Online Rock Salt, indicates.

Apply salt before and after a massive storm for best results, especially when heavy snow, sleet or freezing rain is expected.

In a recent development, “Pre-salting helps prevent ice from bonding to the driveway, while a second application can help break down any ice that forms,” Aaron Strickland, owner of Mr. Trim Lawn & Garden Services, states. “For a typical snowfall, both applications usually aren’t necessary.”.

In a recent development, if only a few inches of snow is forecast, salting after snow removal is likely sufficient. Applying salt before and after a small storm is not only a waste of money, but can damage driveway surfaces, burn lawn edges and generate harmful storm runoff.

In a recent development, “The exact amount of rock salt that you need will depend on how substantial the area is that you are planning to de-ice,” Klimorowski notes. A little goes a long way, and more is not better. A 12-oz. coffee mug filled with salt is enough to treat a 1,000-sq.-ft. driveway. Spread salt evenly, leaving about 3 inches between salt grains. Avoid overapplication, as it can degrade driveway surfaces and harm the environment.

A handheld spreader makes application easier and more consistent, especially for larger driveways. “We try to follow recommended coverage rates and use a spreader wherever possible,” Strickland states. “Too much salt wastes product and can damage surrounding grass and gardens.” If spreading salt by hand, always wear gloves and cascade it for even coverage.

It has been revealed that rock salt is only effective down to ground temperatures of 15 to 17 degrees. Don’t apply more salt if it’s not working, as it’s likely too cold out for it to work. “If your area tends to experience colder temperatures, you may need to find an alternative de-icing product to keep your surfaces safe,” Klimorowski states. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride ice melt products are two common alternatives that remain effective at sub-zero temperatures.

In a recent development, yes, rain will wash away salt rather than dissolve it. It then ends up in storm drains and potentially pollutes local bodies of water.

Rock salt stops working in temperatures below 10 to 15 degrees.

“While it is true that salt will work best if you apply it before the temperatures drop, there is no deadline, and you can always apply it later,” Klimorowski claims.

There’s no guarantee salt will damage your driveway, but you should use it sparingly. Concrete driveways are particularly vulnerable to salt damage.
