Now that working from home has become commonplace, many of us are trying to create quiet environments in which we can complete our work without being distracted by noises from the next room or an overhead apartment.

Whether you’re part of the growing gig economy and looking to soundproof your home office, your teen has rock star dreams, or your 8-year-old has started tap-dancing, you’ll find that a little soundproofing can go a long way toward keeping the peace and quiet at home.

It has been revealed that first, set reasonable expectations. Don’t expect an utterly silent room because you won’t get it. Room soundproofing techniques will reduce sound transfer from one room to another, but they won’t eliminate the loudest noises. Still, by employing the following methods, you can reduce distracting noise to a bearable level. These techniques can be used for any type of room—a home office, a nursery, or a family room, or to create a soundproof bedroom.

Industry observers note that where possible, use the techniques in the adjacent rooms as well as the one you’re looking to soundproof. For example, if an attached garage that’s used as a workshop shares a common wall with the master bedroom, use soundproofing techniques on both the garage wall and the inside of the master bedroom wall for the best results. Learn how to soundproof a bedroom or other room to create a space where noises aren’t distracting.

It has been revealed that creating soundproof walls is most effective when done during construction, but there are several ways to put a damper on ambient and active noise after the fact to make a soundproof room. To minimize noise, consider the two strategies outlined here for how to soundproof a wall.

Mass-loaded vinyl (MLV) is a sound-dampening product used everywhere from nightclubs and recording studios to hockey rinks, and it’s among the best soundproofing materials available. It comes on a roll and costs around $2 per square foot, depending on weight, length, and width. The thicker it is, the better it will be for blocking noise and ending echoes, but thickness, which can range from 1/16 inch to 1/4 inch, may not be listed in product specifications. It may instead be labeled by weight. Half-pound MLV weighs 1/2 pound per square foot of coverage and is 1/16 inch thick; 1-pound MLV is 1 pound per square foot of coverage and is 1/8 inch thick; 2-pound MLV is 1/4 inch thick.

It has been revealed that while MLV can be hung directly on a wall, it performs best when sandwiched between drywall sheets. Doing so also allows you aesthetic options since the usually black, shiny MLV isn’t the most decoratively appealing surface. Keep in mind that MLV, such as Soundsulate, is heavy and awkward to work with. Hanging it is a two-person job, so be sure to enlist a helper.

Tape measureMass-loaded vinylHeavy-duty scissors or utility knifeStep ladderDrywall nailsHammerType X drywall (optional).

Prior to ordering MLV, carefully measure the walls you want to soundproof. Leaving gaps in MLV will drastically compromise its effectiveness, so you’ll want to buy enough for complete coverage from wall to wall and floor to ceiling. When calculating your needs, note that MLV tends to be sold on rolls of 2-foot or 4-foot widths.

It has been revealed that measure a length of MLV that will reach floor to ceiling and then cut out a sheet with the scissors or utility knife. Cutting on top of scrap wood would be wise to protect your floor or work surface.

Recent findings suggest that position the step ladder and put the MLV against the wall starting at either end, working to the other corner. To install it, snug it up against the ceiling, with your helper holding it in place. Using drywall nails and a hammer, attach the MLV to the upper portion of the wall at 12-inch intervals. Then attach the bottom portion at 12-inch intervals, and finally at 12- to 24-inch intervals down the sides of the sheet.

In a recent development, repeat Steps 2 and 3 as required until the entire wall is covered. For the best soundproof wall, butt the MLV right up against the preceding sheet so there are no gaps. You can overlap it for a potentially greater sound barrier, but you’ll have bumps and ridges if you do so. Overlapping is not recommended if you plan to paint, install wallpaper, or install additional drywall panels.

In a recent development, hang drywall on top of the MLV to make the soundproofing twice as effective and give you a surface for paint or other wall covering decor. Or read on for a quick solution to hiding the glossy black vinyl with curtains—a no-commitment decor project that will also enhance soundproofing. Sometimes called “soundproof drywall,” Type X drywall is 5/8 inch thick and fire rated, making it among the best options for noise dampening.

It has been revealed that not for windows only, curtains can create drama on the walls of any room while offering considerable soundproofing benefits. They’re relatively inexpensive and as easy to remove as they are to install. While there are curtains specifically marketed as sound dampening or “acoustic,” blackout and thermal curtains, which are primarily sold to keep light out and warmth in, also provide noise reduction. Don’t let the term “blackout” fool you, though. These curtains come in many colors and styles—it’s the inner liner that provides the blackout/thermal effect. Even heavy fabrics like velvet provide some soundproofing.

Keep in mind that when you double the weight of the fabric, its sound-reduction ability nearly triples. Yet more important than weight is curtain construction; pleated curtains can be three times as effective against noise as those that hang straight. The pleats double the fabric’s thickness in many areas and act as baffles, absorbing sound waves and stopping them in the fabric folds.

In a recent development, remember, sound dampening is the goal, so floor-to-ceiling curtains covering the entire wall will have the most impact. For the best results, hang multiple panels of soundproof curtains to fill the wall. Good options include the BGment Blackout Curtains and Nicetown’s 100% Blackout Curtains. If you’re feeling adventurous, mix colors and patterns for a funky feature wall!

The Pony Dance Blackout Insulated Soundproof Curtains reduced sound by 10 decibels during our hands-on testing. See our full review.

Tape measureSound-absorbing curtains (preferably floor-to-ceiling length)Bathroom scaleHanging system for curtains (rods, wires, or other systems rated for your curtain weight)ScrewdriverScrewsStud finder (optional)Weight-rated drywall anchors (optional)Iron or Steamer.

According to recent reports, measure the walls before purchasing the curtains. When shopping, check package info for the curtains’ weight; you’ll need this to choose rods or another hanging system sturdy enough to hold them. If you’re set on curtains that don’t include the weight on the packaging, weigh them on your bathroom scale at home. Tip: Keep them in the package so they’ll sit easily on the scale.

Recent findings suggest that purchase a hanging system weight-rated for the curtains (packaging or website marketing should tell you the weight load they can handle). If they weigh 40 pounds and the wall to be covered is 12 feet long, you’ll need a rod or hanging system that can handle roughly 3.5 pounds per foot, so keep that weight rating in mind when making your choice. Heavy-duty, ceiling-mount brackets, such as the KXLIFE brackets, will hold the heaviest curtains.

Recent findings suggest that before mounting the hanging system, ensure enough space above it for the top of the curtains to move freely without bunching against the ceiling—a half-inch or inch should do. Locate wall studs with a stud finder, or use proper weight-rated wall anchors before boring into the wall with screws. Affix the rod or hanging system to the walls as recommended by the manufacturer.

These articles will guide you through stud finding and curtain hanging in detail:.

5 Ways to Find a Wall Stud Without Using a Stud FinderHow to Install Curtain Rods.

Sources indicate that iron or steam curtains to remove creases and wrinkles from the packaging. Check the label to see what temperature the manufacturer suggests and iron accordingly.

It has been revealed that hang the curtains on the rod or wire system and then “bunch” them together in equal amounts across the entire wall for a consistent look. When soundproofing a room, keep in mind that pleated, bunched fabric will absorb more sound than flat fabric, so ample curtains are a plus.

Soundproofing a room’s walls will go a long way toward reducing unwanted noise, but for an even quieter room, consider soundproofing other areas. Depending on the type of noise and where it’s coming from, you may also want to add noise-dampening materials to windows, doors, and other areas in the room.

Recent findings suggest that windows let in fresh air and light, but if the window faces a busy urban street, the hustle and bustle of commuters, barking dogs, and emergency vehicles can make it seem as though they’re right in the room. To soundproof a room and mute noise transfer through windows, consider hanging one or more layers of thick curtains over windows, installing storm windows, or using a soundproof weather strip product, such as a draft stopper, to block noise. Soundproofing windows is a vital step in reducing unwanted noise.

According to recent reports, interior doors often have a gap at the bottom that allows air (and noise) to enter a room. Soundproofing a door typically involves using a product that will seal the gap. To soundproof a bedroom door or home office door, try installing a door sweep, such as Suptikes’ Huge Gap door draft stopper.

For renters who aren’t allowed to attach anything to a door, roll up a towel and use it to block the under-door gap to reduce noise transfer. Commercial products are also available, such as the Sunolga draft stopper, and they often come with loops on the ends to hang the item on a door knob when not in use.

Trying to focus on work when the kids are playing in the room overhead is challenging at best, virtually impossible at worst. Reducing noise transfer through a ceiling can be accomplished by soundproofing the floor of the room that lies overhead. For those who live in an apartment and don’t have access to the room above, noise-dampening methods are limited.

Recent findings suggest that homeowners can sandwich a layer of MLV between the existing ceiling drywall and then hang a second layer of drywall. Unlike the MLV method mentioned above to soundproof walls, the simplest way to install MLV overhead is to cut and attach it first to the new drywall panels and then install the panels. Since MLV is heavy, a drywall lift will be necessary for raising the panels.

In a rented apartment, fewer good options are available. Still, renters can reduce ceiling sound transfer using ultra-lightweight foam boards, such as UCreate foamboard. Attach the boards to the ceiling with removable mounting putty, such as Gorilla Mounting Putty, that won’t harm the ceiling.

In a recent development, soundproofing floors by reducing noise transfer from a room below is relatively easy by carpeting the floor or covering hard flooring with one or more large area rugs. When used in combination with the other soundproofing techniques, this may be enough to dampen most noises to a tolerable level.

Homeowners may want to soundproof the ceiling of the room below (described previously) for additional noise reduction.

In a recent development, renters typically cannot structurally modify floors or ceilings, so if adding rugs isn’t sufficient, consider covering hard flooring with a layer of cork, such as Corksidol’s ½-inch-thick cork tiles, to help absorb sound. A large area rug can be added over the cork to protect it and offer a finished look.

In a recent development, water hammer is the product of hydraulic shock, and it can be loud enough to startle anyone who isn’t expecting it. Water hammer occurs when the water is shut off abruptly, and the water supply pipe reacts by jerking and bumping into other pipes or framing members in walls or floors.

If you have access to the offending pipes, slipping some foam pipe insulation around them, such as Foam King Brand foam pipe insulation, will usually stop the problem. Alternatively, a plumber can install a water hammer arrester, such as the Sioux Chief water hammer arrester, to keep the pipe from jerking when the water is turned off.

Industry observers note that hard objects, such as metal and solid wood tables and chairs, do not absorb sound so that noise can bounce around a room. Swapping hard chairs for upholstered chairs and overstuffed sofas will help dampen sound waves and keep them from echoing in the room.

Additionally, following beneficial feng shui practices can also help block noise. Feng shui is a Chinese system of orienting rooms and adding features in a harmonious and pleasing manner. By adding a water feature, the trickling sound of the water will help distract from background noises, and placing live plants throughout the room will help absorb sound while freshening the air.

According to recent reports, effective soundproofing involves using a combination of techniques to block sound transfer from outside a room while absorbing sounds inside the room. The best time to soundproof a home (or room) is during construction, when the walls and floors can be framed in a manner to reduce sound transfer, but unwanted noises can be significantly stifled in existing homes too.

In general, products and materials that are dense and soft will absorb the most noise, including MLV, carpeting, cork, and curtains. Whether you own or rent your home, you don’t have to live with distracting sounds. Learning how to make a room soundproof goes a long way toward maintaining a comfortable living space.

Real egg cartons are not used to block sound. Rather, egg carton-shaped foam, such as Jdejiela‘s egg crate panels, are used to line walls to dampen noise.

The best sound-blocking materials are dense and soft, such as foam and carpeting.

The most effective way is during new construction by utilizing staggered wall studs and joists to create a dead-air space that reduces sound transfer.

It has been revealed that yes, but making a room completely soundproof involves specialized construction practices that create dead-air spaces in floors and walls. Sound reduction is what most are going for.

Industry News: What to Do When Your Toilet Is Bubbling

📅 22 Jan 2018 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • While bubbling or gurgling is a relatively common toilet problem, it’s not an issue you want to ignore.
  • Depending on the severity of the clog, you may be able to clear it yourself with a plunger or an eco-friendly Drano alternative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

While bubbling or gurgling is a relatively common toilet problem, it’s not an issue you want to ignore. When a toilet bubbles, it indicates that negative air pressure (suction) is building up in the drain line, creating an airlock of sorts. Most likely this buildup of air is due to a clog.

Depending on the severity of the clog, you may be able to clear it yourself with a plunger or an eco-friendly Drano alternative. Otherwise, you might have to call a plumber. Is a gurgling toilet dangerous? Not typically, but if the culprit is a broken or collapsed sewer line, it will have to be fixed, and the sooner the better. If the job is put off, waste could back up into toilets, showers, or tubs. The following guide will help you get to the root of toilet bubbling, and offer solutions to the problem.

Clogs typically occur in one of two areas: somewhere in the drain system, which could be close to the toilet or farther down the main sewer line that connects to your community’s sewer system, or in your home’s vent stack (the pipe that allows sewer gasses to escape through the roof). To fix the gurgling toilet once and for all, you’ll need to identify the location of the clog and take steps to remove it.

Recent findings suggest that ridgid’s Power Spin+ has an easy-to-use pull trigger and handle; can be attached to a power drill to dislodge serious blockages. Read the review.

Industry observers note that addressing clogs is key to fixing air bubbles in your toilet—but not all clogs are created equal. A few troubleshooting steps can help you identify whether the solution is DIY-friendly, or if it’s time to call a plumber.

If the cause of the gurgling is in the drainpipe, simply plunging the toilet might create enough pressure to dislodge a light-to-moderate clog. Bathroom fixtures (tub, sink, shower) often connect to the same drain line that runs from the toilet, so you’ll want to seal off these drains with duct tape before plunging. If you plunge without sealing the drains, the pressure plunging creates can escape through other drain fixtures instead of dislodging the clog.

Start by selecting the right plunger, such as the JS Jackson accordion-style plunger, which was a top pick in our researched guide to the best plungers. With the toilet bowl full of water, fit the head of the plunger tightly to the drain hole in the bottom of the bowl. Try to dislodge the clog with 10 to 15 firm pumping motions, then wait to see if the toilet gurgles again. If you don’t have a plunger handy, other ways of unclogging a toilet without one may be just as effective. However, if the gurgling continues, move on to the following steps.

A sewer snake (also known as a plumber’s snake or plumber’s auger) can often remove tough clogs in a drainpipe that plunging can’t manage. Featuring a long cable and a head with cutting blades for chopping through stubborn clogs, the best drain snakes may even have a manual or motorized crank.

If you’re not sure how to snake a toilet, a manual toilet auger ($25 to $100 at home-improvement stores) is inserted into the toilet bowl. As you turn the crank, the head works its way down the drainpipe, cutting through clogs. This type of auger is limited to the distance of its cable reach, generally 5 to 15 feet.

In a recent development, if a clog is so deep in the drainpipe that a small sewer snake cannot reach it, you can upgrade to a motorized auger that will reach 50+ feet, or rent a medium-sized drain cleaner from a home improvement store. Renting the equipment for an afternoon might run you $40 to $50, whereas calling a plumber to snake the drain could run you $150 to $300. Additional repairs, such as removing tree roots from a sewer line or fixing a broken sewer line, may be even costlier.

Since the auger head on a motorized sewer snake is often too large to wind its way through the toilet bowl, the toilet should be removed from its base and the auger inserted into the drainpipe at floor level. When the machine is turned on, the auger will work its way down the line, its razor-sharp blades cutting through tough clogs.

For clogs even deeper in the sewer line—as far out as the middle of your yard—you’ll want to auger the lines from the sewer cleanout, which is just outside of your home, directly over the sewer pipe. To locate the cleanout, check your basement or crawlspace to see where the main sewer line exits your house. Many cleanout pipes extend a few inches above the ground and feature a large PVC cap, but others may terminate just below ground level. You may need to do a little digging to uncover it. Once you’ve removed the cap from the cleanout pipe with an adjustable wrench, auger the sewer line from there. If the toilet gurgling stops, you’ve successfully removed the sewer clog that caused it; if the sounds continue, try troubleshooting the vent stack.

It has been revealed that checking and clearing the vent stack requires getting on the roof, so if you’re not completely comfortable with that, be safe and call the pros. Here’s how to check the vent stack yourself:.

Industry observers note that vent clogs are often caused by leaves and debris, or even the carcass of a small animal that got stuck in the pipe. If the clog is within a few feet of the top of the pipe, you may be able to remove it with a straightened-out wire coat hanger or a toilet brush. Deeper clogs can often be removed by running water from a garden hose in the pipe, which can dislodge the clog, washing it down the pipe and out through the sewer.

In a recent development, can a gurgling toilet fix itself? Unfortunately, the answer is no. If the troubleshooting methods above failed to silence your gurgling toilet bowl, it’s time to call the plumber. Plumbers have specialized emergency plumbing tools and equipment, such as powerful sewer augers that can chop through anything blocking the main sewer line.

It has been revealed that according to Roto-Rooter, gurgling toilets can also indicate that tree roots have grown into the sewer line. If this is the case, repairs are best left to a professional plumber. Professionals can use mini cameras that drop into vent stacks to locate the source of the problem. There’s also a slim chance that the main sewer line in your yard has broken or collapsed, in which case excavation and professional repairs might be necessary.

How to Shovel the Trickiest Surfaces the Right Way, From Pavers to Your Roof

💡 Key Takeaways
  • From lawns to sealed concrete, you might be surprised at how much damage a snow shovel can do.
  • Clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces.
  • “Snow can camouflage uneven areas and patches of ice, posing slip-and-fall risks, particularly when you’re rushing to shovel,” says landscaping expert Jose Lopez.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

From lawns to sealed concrete, you might be surprised at how much damage a snow shovel can do.

Clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces. So, as the days get shorter and colder, it’s important to solidify your shoveling plan before the first snow flies.

“Snow can camouflage uneven areas and patches of ice, posing slip-and-fall risks, particularly when you’re rushing to shovel,” says landscaping expert Jose Lopez. “Being mindful and taking a relaxed, careful approach will help you save money and keep everyone safe all winter long.”.

Ahead, experts walk through how to shovel eleven tricky surfaces around your home, to keep everyone safe, plus prevent costly springtime repairs.

Industry observers note that shoveling gravel is frustrating because those pebbles tend to come up with the snow, then get scattered onto the landscaping. “You will end up cleaning about $150 worth of it off your lawn in the spring,” says grading and paving contractor Scott Flores.

To make life easier, use a plastic shovel, keep the blade about an inch above the gravel and clear the snow in short passes. “You don’t have to expose all of the gravel,” states Lopez. “It’s fine to leave a thin layer of snow behind.”.

Industry observers note that A metal snow shovel blade can actually scratch and gouge concrete. “It can cause $3,000 worth of damage to your pavement in 20 minutes and you won’t know it ’til April,” notes Flores. Initially, the damage “may not look like much, but once water gets under it and freezes, it will cause spalling and make your pavement look 10 years older than it is.”.

Luckily, the fix is easy on this one: always use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel on concrete.

Aliaksandr Bahdanovich/Getty Images.

Aggressive shoveling can damage paint and sealers, even if they’re touted as “scratch-resistant.” “That layer is about three millimeters thick, and your steel shovel will chip it away like you’re peeling your fingernails,” claims Flores.

In a recent development, the fix: use a poly-blade shovel, shovel with a slight upward motion and leave a half-inch of snow for the sun to melt, notes Flores. “Many believe that steel shovels will last longer. Yes they will, but that’s what makes them bad,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you use a deicer, make sure it’s safe for your particular coating, claims Lopez.

Just like with concrete, asphalt seems indestructible, but metal shovels can damage it, especially if it already has imperfections or cracks. So, the best approach is to use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel, and shovel the snow before it partially melts and refreezes.

Recent findings suggest that “Avoid pushing your shovel into cracks or potholes, and don’t bang it against the surface in an attempt to dislodge stubborn ice,” says Lopez. “Instead, choose a deicing product that’s safe for asphalt.”.

A shovel can easily catch the edge of a paver and scratch, break or knock it out of place. To prevent that, use a poly-blade shovel, take shorter shovel strokes, push snow at an angle and slightly raise up the leading edge.

It has been revealed that “Shoveling and deicing aggressively won’t make your job faster or easier, it takes some finesse,” indicates Lopez. Also, use de-icers that are safe for both the paving and jointing material, and inspect the walkway for loose bricks once the snow melts.

After a snow, it can be tricky to tell where the concrete ends and the lawn begins, and one wrong move means damaged grass come springtime. To keep from marring your grass, mark walkway edges with small flags before it snows. While shoveling, keep the blade even with your walkway, versus angling it toward the grass.

Pro-tip: “Slow down and work in short passes near the edges, rather than trying to force the shovel along,” says Lopez. “.

Industry observers note that try not to pile snow on shrubs and other perennials, as that can snap branches. It’s also best to keep deicers and their runoff away from landscaping.

“Before winter arrives, plan where you’ll pile or toss snow to keep it away from sensitive plants,” notes Lopez. “You may find it helpful to use a smaller shovel, which will give you better control over where the snow lands.”.

Industry observers note that also, try not to move soil, which can expose plants to the cold, and never strike frozen branches to remove snow. “Wood breaks more easily than people expect,” says moving professional Leon Schwab.

Aggressive shoveling is sure to damage a deck, regardless of its composition. To preserve yours, use a poly-blade shovel and push the snow in the direction of the boards. If it’s safe to do so, leave a thin layer of snow, instead of shoveling all the way down to bare decking, then apply a deicer that’s recommended for the surface type.

According to recent reports, safety tip: “If wet, heavy snow is accumulating and you notice the deck sagging or hear creaking noises, seek professional advice,” says Lopez. “Don’t continue using the deck if you suspect a structural issue.”.

Stairs are particularly hazardous when its slippery out, and clearing them can be precarious, with snow obscuring their boundaries and confined spaces limiting your range of motion.

To stay safe, “Wear boots with good traction and make sure your staircase is well lit,” says Lopez. “Don’t rush the job. It’s better to take your time and shovel safely.”.

Pro-tip: “Use a small shovel to clear one step at a time and maintain a stable position,” notes Schwab.

In a recent development, sometimes it’s prudent to clear large accumulations of snow from the roof, but it’s also a dangerous job. To stay safe, roofing contractor Andre Kazimierski recommends using a roof rake, which allows you to pull off snow while remaining on the ground. Focus on clearing off as much as you can, but don’t worry about leaving it completely bare, and try not to touch your roofing material.

“Do this sooner rather than later, because if it starts to warm up a bit the snow will become denser and heavier, making it harder to remove,” indicates Kazimierski. “And never walk on your roof when it’s even the slightest bit snowy or icy up there.”.

Obviously, you don’t want to take a shovel to your car, as that would do a lot of damage. Instead, use a snow brush or broom that’s designed to be gentle on vehicle finishes. Flores recommends this one from Snow Joe.

Sources indicate that start by clearing the roof in sections, then move on to the hood, trunk, windows, headlights, taillights and mirrors. You’ll especially want to get the roof and hood fully clear; otherwise, once you start driving, snow can blow up or slide down onto your windshield, obstructing your vision and endangering other drivers. “That ice can fly off your car at 40 miles per hour,” says Flores.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that twenty years ago, I was elevated to chair the antitrust section of the State Bar of Arizona, and I needed a headliner to pack the room for my first event.
  • So I cold-emailed Judge Posner an invitation to address judges, lawyers and law students in Tempe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I thought I'd pass along this tribute, which I thought was moving and apt:.

Dinner with Judge Richard Posner.

Sources indicate that twenty years ago, I was elevated to chair the antitrust section of the State Bar of Arizona, and I needed a headliner to pack the room for my first event. Who in the world of antitrust could draw interest outside that world? The answer was obvious: the closest thing antitrust has to a rock star, Judge Richard Posner.

So I cold-emailed Judge Posner an invitation to address judges, lawyers and law students in Tempe. I doubted he would reply, but he did, rapidly. He would be happy to come—under one condition. I told him to name it.

No antitrust law. Anything but antitrust law.

I agreed, of course. He could have lectured on gardening for all I cared.

In a recent development, we all have our favorite jurists, past and present. Until last week, Judge Posner was my favorite living one. He died at 87. His writing is the reason I became an antitrust lawyer.

In a recent development, thirty years in the law, and I still turn to one trusted source when an issue is opaque or abstract. I run a quick Westlaw search for Judge Posner's take, and the fog lifts.

Recent findings suggest that judge Posner wrote more than 3,300 judicial opinions, and he wrote them to be understood. He embodied what Judge Learned Hand preached nearly a century ago: "The language of law must not be foreign to the ears of those who are to obey it." Posner wrote for the people.

In a recent development, he turned abstract ideas into concrete images. Consider his advice to lawyers who ignored the law that cut against them: "The ostrich is a noble animal, but not a proper model for an appellate advocate." I'm not endorsing the tone, but the point slugs you in the jaw.

According to recent reports, posner made hard things look easy, and he worked hard at it. He confessed to going through up to 20 drafts to give his opinions "a casual, colloquial, and spontaneous appearance." As he put it, "I admit to hypocrisy in working so hard to give the appearance of effortlessness!".

It has been revealed that judge Posner kept his promise and came to Arizona to speak on judicial independence, not antitrust. That night I hosted him for dinner at El Chorro, nestled at the base of Camelback and Mummy mountains.

I was scared. What would I say to Richard Posner for two hours? Convinced I could not carry the conversation alone, I recruited reinforcements, including the Chief Justice of the Arizona Supreme Court and a neurosurgeon.

In a recent development, I opened with a safe question. Had anyone seen any good movies lately?

It has been revealed that posner went first. The last movie he had seen in a theater was Superman. In 1978. Of course. Of course that was the last movie he saw. He did not have time for those trifling pursuits.

But then he leaned in. He and his wife had recently bought the first three seasons of 24 on DVD. Each episode, he marveled, captured one hour in a single day in the life of the protagonist, a man named Jack Bauer. A clock even appeared in the lower left-hand corner of the screen so viewers could watch the minutes tick by in real time. Posner narrated his favorite scenes as Bauer landed in one jam after another and always found a way out.

I have told that story to my law clerks for years. Posner described 24 with the passion and precision he brought to his opinions.

In a recent development, posner was an independent thinker who questioned what everyone else assumed, including his own views. He was a founder of the law and economics movement, building much of it with his longtime friend and collaborator, the economist William Landes.

Posner moved antitrust from the boardroom to the checkout line. He asked whether the alleged anticompetitive conduct created efficiencies and raised or lowered prices for consumers. Courts had not always asked. The Chicago School has largely guided courts and regulators since the Reagan years.

I wrote one book. Posner wrote more than 50, ranging from Law and Literature to Reflections on Judging, all while carrying a full caseload. A 2000 study by Fred Shapiro ranked him the most cited legal scholar of the second half of the twentieth century.

Recent findings suggest that posner's opinions will lift the fog for generations of advocates. A reporter once asked him how law schools could improve legal writing. He noted he would have first-year students read Holmes, Learned Hand and Robert Jackson, then try to write with their clarity. Posner is on that list. Law schools should teach his writing.

In a recent development, A key to the city looks official, but it won't unlock any doors. Here's why cities give them out and what recipients actually receive.

Sources indicate that whether it’s in a movie or real life, everyone has seen or heard of someone receiving an oversized gold key that is a “key to the city.” The ceremony is usually accompanied with a photoshoot, a handshake, and applause. But what does the key actually do?

It has been revealed that cities across the world still hand out these awards, and the tradition goes back much further than most people realize. Learn what a key to the city represents, how the custom began, and what someone actually gets to do with it.

A key to the city is an award that cities give to people they want to honor.

“The Key to the City is presented as a symbol of civic recognition and Philadelphia’s appreciation for individuals whose achievements, service and influence have made a meaningful impact on the city and its people,” according to a release from the City of Philadelphia.

Recent findings suggest that the key is usually decorative, with the city’s name or seal on it. Some come in a display box or with a certificate. Little Rock, Arkansas, considers its key the city’s highest ceremonial honor.

But the key won’t open City Hall or any other public building. It doesn’t give the recipient special privileges or any authority, either. In 2010, Fresh York City tried something different with an art project that gave people working keys to certain locations. Those weren’t the same as the city’s usual honorary keys.

According to recent reports, the tradition goes back to when cities had walls and gates that closed at night. Giving someone a key meant they could come and go without asking permission.

Recent findings suggest that in medieval Europe, leaders also exchanged keys during official visits or military surrenders. Handing over the keys sometimes meant giving up control of a city. Over time, the custom became a way to welcome or honor someone.

Today, cities give keys to athletes, public figures, volunteers, and local residents. Each city has its own rules for who receives one.

In a recent development, philadelphia, for example, honored a resident in 2026 after he walked across the country to support career opportunities for young people. Elk Grove, California, recognizes military accomplishments and acts of heroism, while Little Rock reserves its keys for people who live outside Arkansas.

According to recent reports, mayors usually present the keys, although some cities involve the city council or accept nominations from residents. Recipients get a keepsake and some public recognition, but no special privileges.

#32773. Latest Update: "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents"

Latest Update: "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents"

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I thought I'd serialize my upcoming Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the first Part:.
  • According to recent reports, in certain areas, First Amendment precedent turns out to be quite consistent with original meaning—even though the Court hasn't squarely discussed historical evidence in any detail.
  • It has been revealed that in some situations, this observation may not be accurate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I thought I'd serialize my upcoming Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the first Part:.

According to recent reports, in certain areas, First Amendment precedent turns out to be quite consistent with original meaning—even though the Court hasn't squarely discussed historical evidence in any detail. This might be a fortunate accident, or perhaps a random coincidence in the policy judgments of the modern Court and the Framing generation. But I expect that some at least stems from a phenomenon that Justice Scalia discussed in McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission (1995): "Principles of liberty fundamental enough to have been embodied within constitutional guarantees are not readily erased from the Nation's consciousness. A governmental practice that has become general throughout the United States, and particularly one that has the validation of long, accepted usage, bears a strong presumption of constitutionality.".

It has been revealed that in some situations, this observation may not be accurate. But in others, there really does appear to be a longstanding constitutional understanding that has become so much part of the law that a court that simply follows doctrine will incorporate original meaning. Let me offer three examples.

A. "The Liberty of the Press Is Not Confined to Newspapers and Periodicals".

The Supreme Court has generally held that the First Amendment equally protects all who speak to the public, whether they are professional media (e.g., newspaper publishers or reporters) or nonprofessionals (e.g., leafletters). In this respect, it has treated "the freedom … of the press" as protecting the press as technology—the use of the printing press and its technological heirs—rather than the press as industry, in the sense of people whose daily job is writing for the public.

Now the original articulation of this position in the Supreme Court came in Lovell v. City of Griffin (1938), with little historical analysis:.

The liberty of the press is not confined to newspapers and periodicals. It necessarily embraces pamphlets and leaflets. These indeed have been historic weapons in the defense of liberty, as the pamphlets of Thomas Paine and others in our own history abundantly attest. The press in its historic connotation comprehends every sort of publication which affords a vehicle of information and opinion.

Sources indicate that and this is so even though the Court had shown an interest in Framing-era history. Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson (1931) discussed that history in striking down an injunction against the operation of a "scandalous" newspaper. Grosjean v. American Press Co. (1936) discussed history in considerably more detail in holding unconstitutional a selective tax on certain newspapers.

In a recent development, more recently, Justice Scalia's concurrence in Citizens United v. FEC (2010) offered a bit more historical analysis:.

It has been revealed that the dissent … interpret[s] the Freedom of the Press Clause to refer to the institutional press (thus demonstrating, according to the dissent, that the Founders "did draw distinctions—explicit distinctions—between types of 'speakers,' or speech outlets or forms"). It is passing strange to interpret the phrase "the freedom of speech, or of the press" to mean, not everyone's right to speak or publish, but rather everyone's right to speak or the institutional press's right to publish. No one thought that is what it meant. Patriot Noah Webster's 1828 dictionary contains, under the word "press," the following entry:.

"Liberty of the press, in civil policy, is the free right of publishing books, pamphlets or papers without previous restraint; or the unrestrained right which every citizen enjoys of publishing his thoughts and opinions, subject only to punishment for publishing what is pernicious to morals or to the peace of the state.".

As the Court's opinion describes, our jurisprudence agrees with Noah Webster and contradicts the dissent.

"The liberty of the press is not confined to newspapers and periodicals. It necessarily embraces pamphlets and leaflets…. The press in its historical connotation comprehends every sort of publication which affords a vehicle of information and opinion.".

But this is still predominantly a precedential analysis, with one textual argument and one early republican source.

At the same time, the foundational case in the Court—Lovell—followed 150 years of established practice, to the point that the Court might not have seen the need to do more than just nod to "[t]he press in its historic connotation.".

According to recent reports, as I've laid out elsewhere, Framing-era legal sources, such as cases, treatises, and constitutional provisions, articulated the freedom of the press as extending to everyone, not just to professional newspaper publishers. {See generally Eugene Volokh, Freedom for the Press as an Industry, or for the Press as a Technology? From the Framing to Today, 160 U. Pa. L. Rev. 459 (2012) [hereinafter Volokh, Freedom for the Press]; Eugene Volokh, The Press Clause: Important, Remembered, and Equally Shared, 5 J. Free Speech L. 659 (2025).} Then, starting in the 1820s, courts began to expressly hold that newspaper printers' and editors' rights were equal to everyone else's. In the following decades, that was repeated in case after case throughout the country. By the time Lovell was decided, the principle was well-established in the precedents, and, to my knowledge, unanimously so. The original meaning had made its way into well-settled doctrine and was then ratified by the Court in Lovell.

Industry observers note that the original meaning also fit with practice, which took place in the shadow of the law but which likely also affected the law. In the Framing era, many influential Americans published their views using the printing press, whether in pamphlets or as submissions to newspapers. It would be odd to think that they would have secured special constitutional rights to the just-emerging category of newspapermen, who were in some measure lower status than they were, while denying the same rights to themselves.

According to recent reports, and though those newspapers became relatively more influential in the following centuries, a tradition of leafletting and pamphleteering continued. The Court in 1938 could see the media reality as well as media law and naturally view the nonprofessional leafletter as having the same free press rights as a professional newspaper editor.

The very first case in which the Supreme Court struck down government action as violating constitutional rights of freedom of expression, Stromberg v. California (1931), involved neither the press nor speech in the literal sense. Rather, it involved what one might today call symbolic expression (or expressive conduct)—the display of a red flag as a revolutionary symbol.

But the opinion never discussed why displaying a flag counted as "speech" or "press." The opinion below similarly assumed that symbolic expression was as protected as verbal expression, and so did the parties' briefs in the Supreme Court. The Court had neither before nor since analyzed whether this result is consistent with the original meaning of the free expression guarantees. {See Eugene Volokh, Symbolic Expression and the Original Meaning of the First Amendment, 97 Geo. L.J. 1057 (2009).}.

Likewise, the 1920 California Supreme Court decision in Ex parte Hartman (1920) struck down an earlier law banning the possession or display of flags that represented efforts "espous[ing] for the government of … the United States of America … principles or theories of government antagonistic … to the form of the government thereof as now constituted." The court concluded that Americans have "the right to advocate peaceable changes in our Constitution, laws or form of government," and that therefore "an organization peaceably advocating such changes may adopt a flag … signifying its purpose, and that the display or possession of such flag … cannot be made an unlawful act." The court simply assumed that symbolic expression was constitutionally equivalent to verbal expression, without discussing the matter further.

It has been revealed that but while these assumptions weren't backed by any originalist analysis, they appear to have been fully consistent with the Framing-era understanding that symbolic expression, pictorial expression, and verbal expression were generally treated as functionally equivalent. This equivalence was most often drawn with regard to restrictions on expression, such as defamation law. But it was also the view taken in the early republic with regard to constitutional protections for expression.

Thus, for instance, pre-Revolutionary libel law recognized the category of libel by "pictures, signs, and the like"—meaning through symbols, whether printed or physically displayed—as tantamount to libel by writing. Early American law did the same, extending the same principle to incitement to riot as well. Early treatises drew this equivalence. Early court decisions suggested that pictorial and symbolic expression was potentially protected by free expression guarantees (though subject to the same constitutionally permissible restrictions, such as libel law, as verbal expression).

To offer a particularly vivid illustration, consider the report of Mezzara's Case (1817), apparently the earliest American case involving nonverbal libel—there, a painting of the plaintiff with donkey's ears. The reporter, a Upcoming York lawyer, followed the case with a note hypothesizing what would happen if the painting were an apt commentary on the subject's folly and lack of patriotism. In such a situation, the reporter wrote, "[I]f the painter could show the truth of the matter in evidence, as before described, and that he published and exhibited the picture, 'with good motives and for justifiable ends,' … would he not be justifiable under our statute?".

It has been revealed that the statute the reporter cites—which did allow truth as a defense in libel actions, if the defendant acted with good motives and for justifiable ends—was passed in the wake of the Newly introduced York court's evenly dividing in People v. Croswell (1804) on whether the freedom of the press mandated that the defense of truth be allowed in libel prosecutions. The statute implemented Chancellor James Kent's view of the constitutional rule, which was also the view championed by Alexander Hamilton (as Croswell's lawyer) in one of the last public acts of his life, and was seen as an important protection for the liberty of the press. And just four years after Mezzara's Case, at the next New York constitutional convention, the statute's provisions were adopted as part of the New York Constitution.

The reporter thus saw nothing odd in treating a painting as protected by free expression principles, just as the court saw nothing odd in treating a painting as punishable under libel law principles. Likewise, three-dimensional symbolic expression, such as the raising of a liberty pole, was similarly treated as being potentially constitutionally protected just as pictorial and verbal expression were (though again subject to the possible constitutional limitations imposed on verbal expression).

This equivalence of symbolic, pictorial, and verbal expression unsurprisingly endured as part of the law—most often discussed as to libel law—throughout the 1800s and early 1900s. The Supreme Court, for instance, mentioned in 1845 that libel was a "species of defamation which is effected by writing or printing, or by pictures and signs," and in 1904 quoted a law enacted by the Philippine Commission that offered the same definition. There had been hundreds of similar holdings from state courts, whether explicating the common law or state statutes (and often including "effigies" alongside pictures and signs). Legal treatises had set forth the same principle.

Thus, again, when the cases came before the California Supreme Court in 1920 and the U.S. Supreme Court in 1931, it was natural for the courts and the litigants to casually assume that symbolic expression (there using flags) was likewise treated equivalently to verbal expression for purposes of freedom of expression law. What was accepted in the Framing era continued to be accepted, without any felt need for discussion, in the early 1900s. And here too this conclusion was supported by a long tradition of practice as well as doctrine: Symbolic expression (whether through effigies, processions, visual puns, and the like) was commonplace in the Framing era, and flags and other forms of symbols continued to be used the same way into the 1900s.

New York Times Co. v. Sullivan's "actual malice" requirement has of course been criticized as contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment. But some have also criticized the case on the grounds that it improperly imports freedom of expression principles into civil tort liability. Here too the Court has never tried to explain this particular conclusion on originalist grounds. Likewise, none of the briefs in Sullivan made an originalist argument in favor of applying constitutional limitations to common law civil lawsuits.

In a recent development, nonetheless, here too this may have stemmed from the longstanding understanding, dating back to the Framing era, that freedom of expression guarantees did indeed potentially apply to civil liability. We see that starting with 1802 and 1806 decisions from the Vermont and South Carolina high courts, rejecting liability in part by citing the state equivalents of the Petition Clause. {See generally Eugene Volokh, Tort Liability and the Original Meaning of the Freedom of Speech, Press, and Petition, 96 Iowa L. Rev. 249 (2010) (discussing this).}  And we see that in other cases from 1799 onwards that reasoned that constitutional protections may apply to civil lawsuits as well as to criminal prosecutions, but that libelous speech was constitutionally unprotected against civil liability as well as against criminal punishment. Early commentators took the same view.

And here too the early original meaning turned into well-established constitutional tradition. Throughout the 1800s and 1900s, court decisions routinely assumed that constitutional protections could limit civil liability, though subject to the recognition that there was essentially a First Amendment libel exception for civil as well as criminal liability. By the time of New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964), this position just wasn't particularly controversial, even if the other features of that decision were.

Family Handyman readers share smart solutions for everyday problems in the heart of your home.

From a surprising way to monitor power outages to an epic trick to double your Ziploc bags, Family Handyman readers share smart solutions for everyday problems in the heart of your home.

“The metal wheels of a refrigerator can scratch, dent or gouge just about any flooring surface. Laying down stiff cardboard or a piece of leftover carpet provides an effective barrier, but for the best protection, use a sheet of 1/8‑in. hardboard. The smooth surface protects floors and helps appliances slide into and out of place. —ANTHONY LOMBARDI.

In a recent development, “To find out if power outages ruined the food in your freezer while you were away on vacation, freeze a container of water and rest a penny on top of the ice. If the penny is at the bottom when you get back, it means the power was off long enough to melt the water—as well as thaw (and likely spoil) everything in the freezer. —JOHN NAKAMURA.

Dan Roberts for Family Handyman.

It has been revealed that “If you don’t have a label handy, use a rubber band instead. Stretch it around your Mason jar, then write the contents with a permanent marker. The grippy rubber also makes the jar easier to open. —DAVID KOWALCZYK Picture Frame Message Board I wanted a nicer-looking place for my weekly grocery list and family notes, so I turned a picture frame into a dry-erase board. I simply cut decorative paper to fit the frame and put it behind the glass, creating a surface I can write on with a dryerase marker. —JESSIE DAWSON.

It has been revealed that “For a minor scorch mark on a laminate countertop, skip the abrasive cleaner. Buff it out with car wax or a mixture of toothpaste and baking soda instead.” —ELAINE WHITFIELD.

“Leaky seals around faucets and sink rims can lead to slow but severe damage (they can destroy a countertop, for example). So after installing a newly introduced sink or faucet, dribble water around the area and wait a few minutes. Then get under the sink and look for leaks. —GREGORY PRITCHARD.

“Sometimes it’s tough to mix foods such as old-fashioned oily peanut butter in a small jar by hand. But if you enjoy reaching for a power tool to solve a problem as I do, head out to the garage. As it turns out, the handle of a mixing spoon fits perfectly in the chuck of a cordless drill. —CLIFF MERCER.

According to recent reports, “Build a simple dispenser for your trash bags using 1/2-in. pipe and a few fittings. Screw a floor flange to the cabinet, thread in a 3-in.-long pipe nipple, and then thread a 90-degree elbow onto the nipple. Cut the vertical pipe so it’s a bit longer than the width of the roll of bags. Finally, thread the vertical piece into the elbow and slip on the roll.” —TRAVIS LARSON.

“I turn sandwich-size bags into snack-size bags by heating up an old butter knife with a lighter and slicing the bag in half. The hot knife cauterizes the edges of the two upcoming bags, and the cauterized edges are just as strong as the factory-sealed edges.” —JULIA TRENTON.

Industry observers note that “Need to sharpen a utility knife, pocket blade or scissors but don’t have a sharpening stone on hand? Flip a ceramic mug and use the unglazed ring on the bottom as a sharpener. Hold the blade at a 45-degree angle and slide it across the ring in one direction, from the base to the tip. This won’t replace a proper sharpening kit, but it can quickly clean up a dull edge in a pinch.” —RONALD ALVAREZ.

According to recent reports, “Ice packs are a great way to keep your lunch cool, but they can be expensive to replace if you tend to lose them. To make your own reusable version without spending a lot, soak a sponge in water, then place it in a small resealable plastic bag. Freeze it overnight, then pop it into your lunch container. As the ice melts, the bag holds the water until the sponge reabsorbs it. When you get home, simply refreeze the pack for next time. I like to keep several on hand to use in lunches and coolers, as well as for first aid. They’re inexpensive to make, easy to reuse and help reduce waste.” —TOM SHERIDAN.

Emiko Franzen for Family Handyman.

Sources indicate that “Alphabetizing spices helps you rapidly find what your recipe calls for and makes putting away jars just as fast. Another benefit? You can easily figure out which spices are missing from your pantry, so you’re less likely to discover you’re out of a key ingredient halfway through making a meal. Take a quick glance before grocery shopping to keep staples stocked.” —MARTIN SUTHERLAND.

Recent findings suggest that “When your favorite candle burns too low for a lighter or match to reach the wick, don’t risk burning your fingertips. Instead, light a piece of uncooked spaghetti. It is long enough to reach deep into tall candle holders and burns long enough to light the wick.” —PATRICIA HART.

“For an extra-fresh garbage disposal, toss in a few lemon or lime peels. Run the disposal with cold water until you can’t hear any more grinding, then run it for another 30 seconds (with the water still on).” —GREGORY HOLT.

“A countertop isn’t the best place to keep a recipe while you’re cooking. It takes up counter space, is difficult to read and is bound to get splattered. Instead, use a clothes hanger with pants clips to hang the recipe from a cabinet handle. Open the book or magazine to the desired page (or use a printout), clamp it in place and you have a simple hanging stand. This trick works best with smaller cookbooks, magazines or single-sheet recipes.” —GLENN WHITE.

According to recent reports, “My kitchen drawers used to be an absolute wreck, with pans and dishes crammed in however they’d fit. And seemingly every time I needed something, it was at the very bottom of the drawer. My solution was to cut a piece of 1/8-in. pegboard to the size of the drawer bottom and attach dowels using screws from underneath. Now my pans are organized and easy to access. The 10 minutes it took to build was easily made up with how much frustration it has saved me.” —JIM DAVIDSON.

“Crawling under a kitchen sink to refill the soap dispenser was a hassle, so I tried filling it from above. But when I did, the soap formed an air-lock bubble and overflowed, creating a mess. That’s when I came up with the idea of inserting a drinking straw in the dispenser neck to relieve “bubble block.” Now when I refill the dispenser, the air escapes through the straw and the soap stays where it belongs.” —PAUL SNYDER.

“A dishwasher makes quick work of disinfecting washable toys such as plastic building blocks. Drop the blocks in a mesh laundry bag and run your dishwasher as usual. Remove the bag before the drying cycle, letting the blocks air-dry on a towel. This method also works for items such as seashells, dish brushes, sponges and rags.” —ROBERT VALENTI.

It has been revealed that “If your refrigerator stops dispensing water after you change the filter, make sure the new filter is fully seated. Many people don’t twist it in completely, and one final turn may be all it takes to get the dispenser working again.” —STANLEY BEAUMONT.

“An ironing board with the cover removed can be used as an extra cooling rack when you’re doing a lot of baking. Better yet, it frees up valuable counter space for other kitchen tasks. Just be sure to use pans, paper liners, parchment or some other barrier between baked goods and the board.” —LIZ GRABOWSKI.

Katie Synold for Family Handyman.

It has been revealed that “When the rubber sink baffle on my garbage disposal gets grimy or starts to smell, I switch off the power at the breaker and scrub it with an old toothbrush dipped in hot, soapy water and baking soda. I lift the rubber flaps to clean underneath, where food and grime collect. Then I restore power, rinse it with cold water and run the disposal briefly to flush away the debris.” —CHARLES MCALLISTER.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

Navigating a latest parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

Parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

Diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

It has been revealed that drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

In a recent development, not always. According to the Iowa Statewide Urban Design and Specifications, “One-way angled parking provides fewer spaces than perpendicular for the same length of aisle.”.

According to recent reports, the benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

According to recent reports, there’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

Some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. According to the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Transportation Center, “With the front of their vehicle facing the street, a motorist has improved sight distance when leaving a parking space.”.

In a recent development, back-in parking also lets passengers get out toward the sidewalk and keeps loading and unloading away from traffic. For regular diagonal spaces, drivers should back out slowly and watch for approaching cars and pedestrians. Backup cameras can help, but they shouldn’t replace checking the surrounding area.

Don’t wait until temperatures plummet to perform basic electric and gas furnace maintenance and cleaning. By performing basic furnace cleaning and maintenance tasks now, you can avoid the expensive inconvenience (and danger) of leaving your family without heat during the coldest part of the year. You can also actually prolong the life of your furnace and coax it into operating at maximum energy efficiency.

The following steps can help you learn how to clean a furnace and keep the unit in tip-top shape throughout the winter.

It has been revealed that there are several reasons why it’s necessary for a homeowner to either know how to clean a gas furnace or know when to schedule a professional cleaning with an HVAC expert. However, the most crucial reason is that regular cleaning and maintenance help to extend the life of a furnace and HVAC system, while reducing the number of costly repairs and breakdowns.

Sources indicate that most system failures stem from dirt and dust choking out vital parts like the burners and flame sensors. Learning simple cleaning tasks, like how to clean a flame sensor on a furnace or how to clean the burners, prevents small challenges from turning into expensive emergency repairs. Routine removal of soot, dirt, and dander as part of a furnace tune-up reduces wear and tear on internal components, helping the unit last its full 10- to 15-year expected lifespan.

If you still aren’t sure this is a necessary part of HVAC maintenance, check out this list of additional reasons for why it’s best to clean your furnace.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

It has been revealed that most common furnace maintenance is not complicated—you just have to have a good vacuum cleaner and some basic tools and supplies. However, you do need to take a few precautions, so make sure to read and follow these steps in order to avoid skipping any vital safety measures.

Always turn off the electrical power and fuel supply before you start any furnace project. You can turn off the electricity by either toggling the on-off switch on the unit or turning off the breaker in your breaker panel.

In a recent development, in order to turn off the gas, locate the fuel shutoff valve. The location of the valve varies depending on whether you have an oil or a gas furnace. The valve should either be near the oil tank for an oil furnace or on the incoming gas pipe for a gas furnace. After you locate it, turn the valve off.

Industry observers note that wait several minutes to allow hot components to cool down before opening any panels. While you wait, use a microfiber cleaning cloth to wipe down the exterior of the furnace.

With a screwdriver, unscrew and remove the upper and lower service panels to gain access to the interior cavity of the furnace.

It has been revealed that the Ridgid vac has a 7-foot heavy-duty locking hose and a 15-foot cord and made quick work of both wet and dry messes in our tests. Read the review.

Locate the small metal flame sensor rod near the burner assembly (often marked with a red or white connector). Unscrew and carefully pull the sensor out. Then gently scrub away soot or white-gray oxidation using fine-grit sandpaper or a wire brush until the metal shines. When you are done, wipe it clean and screw it back in.

Basic furnace filters are designed to trap dust, dirt, and airborne particulates before they can enter the furnace and potentially damage its components. As filters become full, they become unable to filter the air. While some filters can be cleaned, while others need to be replaced. During the heating season, clean or replace the furnace filter every 1 to 3 months.

Detach the burner cover and carefully slide or lift the burners out if they appear dirty or rusty. Brush any surface debris away with a soft-bristle brush or wash them in warm soapy water. After washing, rinse the burners thoroughly and dry them completely with compressed air before reinstalling.

Inspect the blower wheel fins for heavy dust buildup with a flashlight or your phone camera. If you see dust, use your vacuum to clean loose dust from the fins using a brush attachment. However, when the blower wheel is heavily caked in grime, it’s best to call a technician for a deep wash. It isn’t recommended for an inexperienced DIYer to remove the blower, so it’s best to stick to light vacuuming and dusting for this part of the process.

Put all access panels and doors back into place, ensuring any safety door switches are properly depressed, then turn the gas valve back on (parallel to the pipe) and restore power at the breaker or switch. Set your thermostat to Heat and watch to make sure the igniter glows, the gas catches smoothly into clean blue flames, and the blower kicks on.

Ideally, you should clean the furnace once a year to keep it in top condition before the fall heating season begins. It also is a good idea to perform a quick clean in the spring, vacuuming up any dust or soot. Proper care and maintenance will help prolong the life of your furnace, and keep it running at peak efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that strategy to replace or clean your furnace air filters every 1 to 3 months, clean the furnace about once a year in the spring, and hire a pro to inspect and deep clean it every fall. Also, consider having your home’s air ductwork cleaned every 3 to 5 years.

Although basic furnace maintenance can be handled by most homeowners, it makes sense to hire a professional for some tasks. For example, if you’ve noticed the furnace rumbling and can’t figure out why, then it’s best to call a pro for some on-site troubleshooting.

Additionally, there are some cleaning jobs that should be left to the experts, so instead of trying to figure out how to clean a furnace heat exchanger, remove a blower, or clean the coils, it’s better to book a deep furnace cleaning with a trained furnace technician. Save yourself some time and potential problems by calling an HVAC pro for any of the following challenges.

According to recent reports, your furnace is a major investment in your home and your family’s comfort and safety. Regular cleaning and maintenance can save you money in the long run, because it will maximize the effective lifespan of your unit. Whether you are looking to maximize the efficiency and performance of a fresh or existing unit, just a couple of hours of cleaning and maintenance every year will help keep your investment in tip-top shape and make sure your family stays comfy and cozy during the colder winter months.

Sources indicate that cleaning, changing filters, and lubricating your furnace are fairly simple steps in a process that really doesn’t take long. For a first-timer, it might take a few hours, since you might be dealing with unfamiliar equipment. After you have done it a few times, however, a full furnace clean should only take 1 to 2 hours. Changing the filters is even faster, and it only takes a few minutes to ensure that your air is clean and filtered.

According to recent reports, you should clean or service your furnace when you notice weak airflow, strange smells, or a spike in your energy bills. Here are other common signs that you should clean your furnace: • The furnace turns on and off rapidly when there are dirty flame sensors, clogged filters, or blocked burners that cause the unit to overheat.• Banging, screeching, or rattling sounds can mean the blower wheel is caked in debris or motor bearings need attention.• If dust settles quickly around your furniture or return grilles soon after cleaning, your filter or blower compartment is likely overloaded.• The burner flame should burn steady and blue. A yellow flame means poor combustion and possible soot or carbon monoxide buildup.• An increase in sneezing, congestion, or dust-related irritation when the heat runs means the system is circulating allergens instead of trapping them.

Failing to clean your furnace can lead to carbon monoxide leaks, higher energy bills, and system breakdowns. Dirt and soot can cause incomplete combustion or crack the heat exchanger, releasing invisible, odorless, and deadly carbon monoxide gas into your home.Thick accumulations of dust, lint, and debris near the burners, wiring, or moving components can overheat and spark an electrical or mechanical fire. Also, a dirty filter or blocked flame sensor can cause the furnace to repeatedly turn on and off in short bursts, failing to heat your home evenly. Additionally, clogged air filters and dirty internal parts block airflow, forcing the system to work harder and consume more fuel or electricity to heat your space. Neglected filters stop trapping dust, pollen, pet hair, and allergens, which then circulate through your vents and trigger asthma or allergy symptoms. All of this added strain wears out the blower motor, flame sensor, and other mechanical parts much faster, significantly cutting down the typical 15- to 20-year lifespan of a furnace.

In a recent development, the average cost to clean a furnace ranges from about $70 to $400, depending on the type and location of your furnace. Typically, oil furnaces will cost more since they require deeper cleaning, and any units located in the attic or crawlspace will naturally cost more due to the difficulty accessing these areas.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

It has been revealed that ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

Ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

In a recent development, ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

Industry observers note that de-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy says.

Sources indicate that though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

“Fresh concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy says. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy states.

Recent findings suggest that all ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher indicates.

Industry observers note that natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

Recent findings suggest that ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

According to recent reports, electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice swiftly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

It has been revealed that “The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher says, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

Recent findings suggest that regular sealing protects cement-based products. “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy says. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

It depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher claims, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher states, as they still contain salt.
