    Breaking: Justice Department Introduces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today the Department of Justice revealed coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.
    • “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M.
    • “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” remarked Assistant Attorney General A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today the Department of Justice revealed coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

    “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement demonstrates that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

    “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” remarked Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

    “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” noted First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

    “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

    “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

    Sources indicate that “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” remarked Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

    Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

    In a recent development, today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

    North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

    During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

    The North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

    The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

    Industry observers note that the effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

    The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

    Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

    Recent findings suggest that efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

    The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

    • Industry observers note that from Judge Trina Thompson (N.D.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that from Judge Trina Thompson (N.D. Cal.) today in Nat'l Federation of Federal Employees v. U.S. Dep't of Agriculture:.

    In a recent development, the Court ORDERS that the Secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages. She "[m]ust stop if a colleague asks [her] to stop," she "[c]annot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances," and she "[c]annot use official authority to pressure subordinates." USDA Secretary's Memorandum 1078-019. She may "[d]iscuss [her] religious beliefs with interested colleagues," "[s]hare why [her] faith is meaningful to [her]," "[p]olitely invite coworkers to religious services or events," "[e]xpress religious viewpoints during appropriate conversations." This Court expresses no view whatsoever on what the Secretary can and cannot do in her personal capacity….

    On July 4, 2025, Secretary [of Agriculture Brooke] Rollins sent an email from her official email account celebrating Independence Day. The message was sent to all USDA employees. Her message concluded with a written statement, "May God continue to protect the United States of America and may His favor shine over all her land." On November 26, 2025, Rollins sent a Thanksgiving message from her official email account to all USDA employees, attributing the first Thanksgiving in part to "gratitude towards a loving God.".

    Industry observers note that the complaint identifies two subsequent communications as expressly promoting Christianity. On December 23, 2025, Rollins emailed USDA employees a Christmas message containing a video in which she stated that "The spirit of generosity flows from the very first Christmas when God gave us the greatest gift possible, the gift of his Son and our Savior Jesus Christ, who came to free us from our sins and open the door to eternal life. This is the reason for the season….".

    On April 5, 2026, she sent an Easter email addressed to "All USDA Employees" which read:.

    Happy Easter – He is Risen indeed!

    Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind.

    Recent findings suggest that from the foot of the Cross on Good Friday to the stone rolled away from the now empty tomb, sin has been destroyed. Jesus has been raised from the dead. And God has granted each of us victory and upcoming life. And where there is life — risen life — there is hope.

    Sources indicate that no matter the very real trials and hardships we face, fear and sin and death do not get the last word. Because on Easter morning, "Hell took a body, and discovered God. It took earth, and encountered Heaven. It took what it saw, and was overcome by what it did not see." Now that is reason to rejoice!

    And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for.

    Sources indicate that please know how amazed and grateful I am for the hard work each of you do to support our shared mission here at USDA. I hope you and your loved ones have a truly blessed and happy Easter. May God continue to bless you, your families, and our exceptional country, One Nation, Under God.

    At the top of the email, Secretary Rollins included an illustration of a stone rolled away from Jesus' tomb with the words "Christ is Risen" written above the illustration.

    In a recent development, plaintiffs allege that Rollins has not sent comparable messages acknowledging other religions' holidays. They contrast her communications with USDA's November 20, 2025 guidance on religious expression, which provides that officials "[c]annot use official authority to pressure subordinates" regarding religious beliefs and "[m]ust stop if a colleague asks [them] to stop." They further allege that Rollins defended the Easter message publicly and is likely to send similar communications marking future Christian holidays.

    It has been revealed that each individual plaintiff received and read the challenged messages. Plaintiffs allege that they are expected to read communications from the Secretary because those communications may contain consequential workplace information. Other messages have addressed agency reorganization, employee relocation, changes to USDA's civil rights program, shutdown planning, and the Deferred Resignation Program; holiday messages have historically included administrative-leave announcements.

    The individual plaintiffs allege that the messages convey a preference for employees who share the Secretary's Christian beliefs, make them feel excluded, and pressure them to conceal their own beliefs or appear to share hers. They fear workplace disfavor and retaliation for objecting; the complaint also alleges that supervisors have warned that objections would result in "trouble." Plaintiff Poopatanapong alleges that she no longer feels safe discussing a Buddhist holiday she celebrates; Roberts, an atheist, feels silenced; and Wolfe, a Pagan, feels pressure to appear Christian to advance professionally. alleges that its USDA members likewise received the messages, felt compelled to read them, and experienced pressure to accept the Secretary's beliefs while withholding their own.

    The court held that plaintiffs' Establishment Clause were likely violated:.

    The Establishment Clause protects religious freedom by "command[ing] a separation of church and state." Kennedy v. Bremerton Sch. Dist., 597 U.S. 507, 558–59 (2022) (citing Cutter v. Wilkinson, 544 U.S. 709, 719 (2005)). [Note that this quote is actually from Justice Sotomayor's dissent in Kennedy, though it appears in the Cutter majority. -EV] At its core, this means forbidding "sponsorship, financial support, and active involvement of the sovereign in religious activity." As the Supreme Court acknowledged in Kennedy, the Establishment Clause does not "'compel the government to purge from the public sphere' anything an objective observer could reasonably infer endorses or 'partakes of the religious.'" However, courts must be cautious to ensure that "what might begin as a tolerant expression of religious views" does not "end in a policy to indoctrinate and coerce.".

    To determine whether government action violates the Establishment Clause, the Court must "focus[ ] on original meaning and history" of the First Amendment. That is, this Court's must be guided by "historical practices and understandings" of the relationship between government and religion in America. Pursuant to this approach, any practice that was "accepted by the Framers and has withstood the critical scrutiny of time and political change" does not violate the Establishment Clause. The analysis does not end merely because a practice has been observed in the past. The history and tradition test requires this Court to look to the "uninterrupted practice" of law in our nation's traditions.

    Traditionally, the hallmark of government conduct violative of the Establishment Clause is the presence of some form of coercion upon its citizens.

    Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, the two Founders most instrumental in the drafting and ratification of the Religion Clauses of the First Amendment, articulated a founding-era concern broader than direct, compelled sectarian practices. Madison, for example, expressed concern that even instances of governmental "recommendation[]" concerning religion "naturally terminate[] in a conformity to the creed of the majority []." Jefferson expressed concern about indirect forms of coercion such as conduct which might invite "some degree of proscription perhaps in public opinion." Most fitting, in his "Memorial and Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments" drafted in 1785, Madison questioned the ends sought by the promotion of a sectarian underpinning to our country's political foundation: "Who does not see that the same authority which can establish Christianity, in exclusion of all other Religions, may establish with the same ease any particular sect of Christians, in exclusion of all other Sects?" His guidance, contained in the same writings: "Such a Government will be best supported by protecting every Citizen in the enjoyment of his Religion with the same equal hand which protects his person and his property; by neither invading the equal rights of any Sect, nor suffering any Sect to invade those of another." The Founders may have lacked the foresight to account for contemporary technological advances, but the principles embedded in our First Amendment ring as true today. As difficult as the task may be, below, this Court faithfully applies the founding-era's understanding of the Establishment Clause to the modern-day circumstances giving rise to this litigation….

    According to recent reports, after reviewing and weighing the Establishment Clause jurisprudence, the Court finds that Secretary Rollins appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion. Here, three factors inform the Court's conclusion that the Secretary's conduct was coercive: (1) her position of authority, (2) the use of her official email to send messages to all USDA employees, and (3) the alienating language contained in the emails to employees who did not share her religious tenets. [Detailed discussion of factors 1 and 2 omitted for space reasons. -EV].

    It makes no difference that the emails did not single out dissidents, disparage those who did not share the Secretary's beliefs, or indicate work-related decisions would be influenced by an employees' reaction to the emails. The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that "immense social pressure" can result in a finding of coercion. Such pressure is demonstrated here…. While social pressure alone is not state coercion because "mature adults … presumably are not readily susceptible to religious indoctrination or peer pressure[,]" the totality of the circumstances here demonstrates such immense pressure to amount to coercion….

    According to recent reports, the Court does not purport to regulate the religiosity of the Secretary—nor could it. "A relentless and all-pervasive attempt to exclude religion from every aspect of public life could itself become inconsistent with the Constitution." Nor does this Court generally condemn the expression of religious sentiments. Instead, this Court requires the Secretary to observe her own directives. USDA Secretary's Memorandum 1078-019. The April 5, 2026, and December 23, 2025, messages go too far. They suggest acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure; a pressure of conformity sufficient to raise an Establishment Clause violation….

    #32743. Retrospective Voting and the 2026 Election

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1635 w)

    Retrospective Voting and the 2026 Election

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1635 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, in my book Democracy and Political Ignorance  and various other writings going all the way back to my very first academic article (published in 1998), I have warned of the dangers of widespread voter ignorance.
    • Retrospective voting is probably the most often-used information shortcut, and the one most cited by scholars who argue that voter ignorance isn't much of a problem.
    • If things are going well, you vote to reelect them to continue their good work.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, in my book Democracy and Political Ignorance  and various other writings going all the way back to my very first academic article (published in 1998), I have warned of the dangers of widespread voter ignorance. And I have argued that "information shortcuts" - small bits of knowledge that supposedly make up for ignorance about details - are generally ineffective or even counterproductive. Thus, I should acknowledge that one of those shortcuts - retrospective voting - worked fairly well in the recently concluded 2026 election. At the same time, the problem of political ignorance remains a grave menace.

    Retrospective voting is probably the most often-used information shortcut, and the one most cited by scholars who argue that voter ignorance isn't much of a problem. The basic idea is simple: to be a good voter you don't need to know much about government and public policy. You just need to know whether things are going well or badly under the rule of the incumbents.

    If things are going well, you vote to reelect them to continue their good work. If badly, you vote to "throw the bastards out." Then you elect a fresh set of bastards in their place; but the new bastards will hopefully know they need to do a good job, else they will get thrown out in their turn, at the next election. As Ronald Reagan famously put it during the 1980 election, "Next Tuesday all of you will go to the polls… I think when you make that decision it might be well if you would ask yourself: Are you better off than you were four years ago?".

    I and other critics have long pointed out that, when ignorant voters use the retrospective voting shortcut, they often end up rewarding and punishing incumbents for things they did not cause (usually short-term economic trends), while ignoring more subtle long-term concerns. In addition, they often don't know which officials are responsible for which issues, and tend to overlook the possibility that the opposition party's policies will be as bad or worse.

    Nonetheless, retrospective voting actually worked pretty well in the 2026 election. As I noted in a previous post, polls show that many voters punished the Republicans for high prices caused by Trump's tariffs,  the failed Iran War, and the administration's cruel campaign of mass deportations (which particularly angered Hispanic voters in key states and congressional districts). One can also add the concern of corruption, which polls  indicate also had a big impact.

    The Republicans really were responsible for all three of these policies. They weren't caused by exogenous factors outside of Trump's control. And the policies really did have massive negative effects in raising prices, an unsuccessful war, and massive cruelty and violations of civil liberties caused by the deportation campaign. The scope and effects of corruption are harder to measure. But this administration may be the most corrupt in American history. And, on all four complications, the Democrats are likely to be at least somewhat better.

    It has been revealed that but while retrospective voting worked reasonably well in the 2026 midterm election, we cannot conclude that the problem of political ignorance doesn't matter, or even that it's overblown. Rather, the shortcut was effective primarily because of the large and obvious nature of Trump's failures.

    Industry observers note that along with other scholars, I have long recognized that retrospective voting can be effective if incumbents screw in ways that have large and obvious bad effects - ones that even very ignorant voters can easily see and understand. For example, I often cite economist Amartya Sen's famous finding that mass famines never or almost never occur under democracies (even as they happen much more often under dictatorships). Even ignorant voters will notice a famine is going on, blame incumbents for it, and vote accordingly.

    It has been revealed that trump's failures over the last two years weren't quite as bad as a mass famine. But they were nonetheless large (including a major war and  the highest tariff schedule since the Great Depression), highly visible, and many of their effects were easy to understand. It isn't hard to notice that massive tariff increases cause prices to rise. The war and its effects on prices were also highly visible. Images of brutal deportations and resulting civil liberties violations were all over the news. Most voters probably didn't know about the details of the administration's corruption. But there was so much of it, that most probably heard at least something about it.

    Sources indicate that many policy failures are far less readily apparent than that. And ignorant voters are therefore likely to overlook or misunderstand them. It's not hard to find examples even in the 2026 election itself. To take a particularly crucial case, the US faces a massive looming fiscal crisis, caused in large part by the combination of an aging population and out-of-control entitlement spending. Yet most candidates of both parties largely ignored this problem, and promise continued massive spending, and avoiding tax increases for almost everyone, except perhaps a few billionaires and other very wealthy people. They could do that because surveys show most voters are ignorant about our fiscal situation and especially don't realize the key role of entitlement spending.

    Recent findings suggest that voters' justified negative reaction in 2026 to tariffs, mass deportations, corruption, and the Iran War also highlight the failure of information shortcuts in the 2024 election. At that time, it was evident to informed observers that Trump would seek to institute massive tariffs and cruel deportation policies. Indeed, I myself was among those who cited them as among the principal reasons to oppose Trump in that election. Large-scale corruption was also predictable, given Trump's long history of skullduggery. Yet swing voters got these issues wrong - despite the fact that high prices were a major issue in 2024, and tariffs and mass deportations would predictably raise them (as I also pointed out at the time).

    Sources indicate that the Iran War was admittedly less predictable. Trump even promised to avoid newly introduced wars. But his well-documented combination of ignorance and impulsiveness meant that returning him to office created a significant risk of a foreign policy crisis spiraling out of control.

    And on all these issues, it was predictable (and predicted by many, including me) that Trump 2.0 would surround himself with cronies and loyalists likely to indulge his worst instincts. No longer would he be constrained by "adults in the room," as occasionally happened during his first term.

    Recent findings suggest that thus, while an information shortcut worked well in 2026, it's important to recognize that was only necessary because shortcuts failed miserably in 2024, which was an only modestly more difficult situation. In that earlier election, we did not yet see the effects of Trump's awful second-term policies. But most of those policies and effects were readily predictable by any moderately well-informed observer. Yet most swing voters were much more ignorant than that, and thus instead voted to punish Democrats for high prices, ignoring the high likelihood that electing Trump would make that problem worse, not better.

    In addition, as I emphasized in my November 2024 post on voter ignorance in that year's election, a combination of ignorance and bias led many voters to underestimate the significance of Trump's assault on basic norms and principles of liberal democracy.

    In a recent development, it is also important to remember that the problem of voter ignorance is not just that it leads voters to make "wrong" choices between the options put before them. It also makes those options worse in the first place. As I have long argued in my book and elsewhere, political ignorance also makes those options worse in the first place. Politicians and campaign strategists know they face a largely ignorant electorate, and act accordingly. Sweeping the fiscal crisis under the rug is just one of many examples of that tendency. Even if information shortcuts consistently helped voters choose the lesser of the evils before them (which, sadly, they don't!), ignorance would still make those options much more evil than they would be otherwise.

    Recent findings suggest that trump is a particularly egregious long-time exploiter of political ignorance, which played key roles in his rise and return to power. But more conventional politicians also routinely exploit it, as Barack Obama did, for example. For those keeping score, I have been arguing that political ignorance is a serious danger for over 25 years, under both Republican and Democratic administrations, and through many changes in the political winds.

    According to recent reports, the  2024 election led me to conclude that voter ignorance was an even more serious problem than I previously thought. This year's election is, perhaps, a data point for the other side. But whether or not the problem is worse than I thought before 2024, it continues to be a serious danger.

    There is no easy fix for widespread voter ignorance. I assessed  various possible options in my 2023 book chapter on "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance, and in Chapters 5-7 of Democracy and Political Ignorance. I think the most promising approach make fewer decisions at the ballot box and more by "voting with your feet," where incentives to seek out information and use it wisely are better. I also argue in both works that the idea of simply paying voters to increase their knowledge deserves more attention. But any remedy will take time, and we may need a combination of several strategies, not just one.

    In sum, the 2026 election is an example of retrospective voting working relatively well. But we should not conclude this shortcut - or any other - is a good general solution to the problem of widespread political ignorance.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I previously wrote about the Trump Justice Department's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate election results, and the district court ruling rejecting it.
    • Industry observers note that today, as reported by prominent election law scholar Rick Hasen, DOJ filed a brief in the US Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit seeking to dismiss the case.
    • In a recent development, this brings to an end a lawsuit that was always a turkey of a case (though perhaps calling it that is an insult to turkeys!).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I previously wrote about the Trump Justice Department's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate election results, and the district court ruling rejecting it. The Trump DOJ argued that blocking the  results was necessary to prevent "voter confusion" caused by the presence of two candidates with very similar names on the ballot. As I  explained previously, Republican candidate Dan J. Sullivan can potentially be confused with Dan S. Sullivan (the incumbent GOP senator), and some voters might have accidentally chosen Dan J. even though they intended to back Dan S.

    Industry observers note that today, as reported by prominent election law scholar Rick Hasen, DOJ filed a brief in the US Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit seeking to dismiss the case. They also want the district court ruling vacated for procedural reasons (I will not opine on whether that's warranted).

    In a recent development, this brings to an end a lawsuit that was always a turkey of a case (though perhaps calling it that is an insult to turkeys!). As explained in my post on the district court ruling and in an excellent amicus brief filed by Rick Hasen, the case never had any merit, and a court decision ruling in its favor would have set a dangerous precedent.

    In addition, the election results show that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola got an absolute majority of the vote (about 50.1%), more than both Dan Sullivans and all other candidates combined. Thus, even if all of the 1.7% of voters who chose Dan J. actually intended to back Dan S., it made no difference. Alaska's system of ranked choice voting (under which, if no candidate gets a majority in the first round, votes get reallocated) might have further reduced any problem. But no reallocation took place here, because Peltola got an absolute majority to begin with. This is likely what led DOJ to finally thrown in the towel.

    As noted in one of my earlier posts about the case, Democrats may well deserve blame for seeking to deceive voters in this way, even though it was never likely to change the result (evidence indicates Dan J. may have gotten on the ballot as part of a Democratic effort to siphon off voters from Dan S.). But for reasons outlined in the same post, this kind of thing is far from the worst example of exploitation of voter ignorance.

    In a recent development, peltola's win was mostly just part of the broader "Blue tsunami" which saw the Democratis gain 9 Senate seats, including in several traditional red states. But perhaps Peltola got over the top because of the immense popularity of her pet lizard! We could use more lizards on Capitol Hill.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar" is the title of a newly introduced and important film designed to help judges and legal professionals understand the mechanics and features of modern firearms, including the AR-15 semiautomatic rifle. The film is available on YouTube and on Rumble. Following my brief introduction, firearms expert Richard Vasquez takes the center stage. After 21 years in the Marine Corps as an advanced gunsmith and ordnance officer, Mr. Vasquez served for 14 years in the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), including time within the Firearms Technology Branch. He is now a firearms consultant.

    It has been revealed that this is a critical time to inform the bench and the bar about the operation of the AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles, given the ongoing legal fights over modern semiautomatic firearms including the pending Supreme Court cases of Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins. This film sticks to the facts about the operations and mechanics of modern firearms without touching upon any of the legal or political debates about the AR-15. It does a particularly good job explaining the various features found on most AR-15 rifles and does a great job explaining the differences between semiautomatic firearms and other types of modern firearms, including fully-automatic machine guns.

    Industry observers note that the film was written, directed and produced by law professor and Second Amendment scholar Mark W. Smith, who was most recently seen discussing firearms and the American Revolution on the Federalist Society annual convention panel "When in the Course of Human Events" (at 22:30).

    It has been revealed that the film begins with a historical overview of the development of firearms, from single-shot flintlocks to today's semiautomatics. The film describes the basic components of firearms and rifles, in particular. It explains what makes gas-operated semiautomatic rifles different from lever action, bolt action and pump action rifles. The film then goes on to show in great detail how a gas-operated semiautomatic rifle operates.

    It has been revealed that spoiler alert:  I suspect that one of the film's biggest contributions to the public discourse on semiautomatic firearms will be its easy-to-understand graphics and animations. Thanks to many colorful images, video clips, animations as well as Vasquez's break downs of modern firearm mechanics and operations, I suspect this film will become a valuable teaching tool for people interested in firearms including judges and legal professionals.

    According to recent reports, getting to the technical aspects, Mr. Vasquez explains the AR-15 firing mechanism, beginning with the insertion of a cartridge into the chamber, pulling of the trigger, activation of the sear, release of the bolt and firing pin, striking of the primer, explosion of the powder, discharge of the bullet, bleeding of gas causing the bolt carrier group to retract, elimination of the spent cartridge, and insertion of a fresh cartridge from the magazine to the chamber, thus beginning a new firing cycle. Easy to follow diagrams of each process in that order simplify and bring to life what happens each step of the way.

    Industry observers note that next, Mr. Vasquez moves onto the outward features typical of the AR-15 platform. The telescoping stock allows the shoulder stock to be adjusted for different statures, such as two spouses, or seasonal clothing, like an overcoat while hunting. The pistol grip and straight-line stock reduce recoil and muzzle jump, allowing a second, more accurate shot. The handguard (barrel shroud) with Picatinny Rail facilitates various attachments like iron sights, scopes, and flashlights. A threaded barrel can be equipped with a flash suppressor to reduce blindness when firing at night or with a muzzle brake to lesson recoil.

    According to recent reports, two aspects of the operational process are worth emphasis. First, nothing about the AR-15 rifle itself dictates the number of rounds it will fire before needing to reinsert a latest magazine. That depends on the magazine, which may hold 5, 10, 20, or 30 rounds. Second, while firing a shot automatically loads a new cartridge into the chamber, firing the next shot requires that the trigger be pulled again. That distinguishes a semiautomatic from a fully automatic, aka a machine gun, which requires only the trigger to be depressed and held down to fire all rounds in the magazine.

    It's my belief that "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar" will become the definitive documentary on the mechanics of the AR-15 and modern semiautomatic rifles.

    Recent findings suggest that western civilization is facing a crisis driven by mass immigration from the Muslim world. If these patterns persist unchecked, they threaten to “change and corrupt the national spirit” of America.[REF]The growing prevalence of Islamic culture presents a host of practical problems for American society. Although Islamification is not yet a national threat on the scale seen in Europe, select urban centers and rural communities have started to become transformed by the influx of unassimilated Muslim immigrants. According to Lauren Gilbert, many of the Somali diaspora in Lewiston do not wish to assimilate into America’s “majority culture.” “Many Somali elders,” she reports from interviews, “view assimilation into the American mosaic as a threat to the very survival of the Somali people.” Accordingly, the Somali elders chose Lewiston, in part, “because they believed that they could raise their children and practice their religion in relative peace, free from unwanted outside influences.”[REF]Examples such as Lewiston’s Somali diaspora underscore how America’s embrace of multiculturalism has made it impossible to accommodate Islam without altering the character of the nation itself. As Gilbert acknowledges, “from a multiculturalist perspective, the desire not to assimilate and thus to lose one’s cultural and religious identity is a legitimate choice that the host society should respect and accommodate.”[REF] Many Muslim immigrants and their children reject the traditional “melting pot” settlement that integrated previous waves of immigrants into a unified American national identity.A 2026 op-ed in The Washington Post by Shadi Hamid, a senior fellow at Georgetown University, exemplifies this view. Hamid argues against the premise that “a minority community’s right to be in the United States depends on its willingness to converge with the cultural mainstream.”[REF] In Hamid’s view, “America was not founded on the assumption that its citizens would eventually come to agree on foundational questions.”This sentiment is widely shared by prominent Islamic organizations across America. The Council on American-Islamic Relations’ (CAIR’s) 2026 Civil Rights Report explicitly criticizes the old American tradition on immigration that sought to “preserve the ideal of U.S. homogeneity” and all attempts to restore the vision of America as united by a “single heritage.”[REF] To this end, the report asserts CAIR’s commitment to protecting Muslims’ “right to be different.” A 2009 article reposted by CAIR, which includes “assimilation” in a list of terms “not to use with Muslims,” is further indicative of this prevailing sentiment.[REF] In this same spirit, the Islamic Circle of North America declared in a statement issued ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11 that they “reject the premise that American belonging is contingent on loyalty tests or displays of patriotism.”[REF]Contrary to Hamid’s supposition, the Western tradition has long maintained that a republic depends, as Cicero would say, upon a fundamental agreement on justice and the common good. Mass immigration from civilizations with radically different political theologies and conceptions of justice, whose adherents refuse to adopt American cultural mores and the American tradition of ordered liberty, threatens the very existence of that tradition.The old tradition on immigration was rooted in the conviction that “America must be kept American.”[REF] That tradition recognized that too much immigration that is too disparate in culture, religion, and mores would change America’s regime of natural rights, self-government, and ordered liberty into something both foreign and undesirable. This precedent was subsequently affirmed by the Reconstruction Congress and by several decades of judicial precedents from the early 20th century. Together, these various writings, debates, speeches, statutes, and court opinions form a consistent political tradition that endured for 175 years, beginning with the Naturalization Act of 1790 until the passage of Hart–Celler in 1965. Restoring this tradition offers the surest guide for navigating the challenges posed by mass immigration. What follows is a reconstruction of this tradition’s prevailing ethos.The Founders on Immigration and Republican CitizenshipThe Founding Fathers did not directly address the question of Muslim immigration or the compatibility of the Islamic faith with American society. The dilemmas of late modernity, in many respects, are unique in the history of the nation. As a result, modern Americans cannot simply look back to the Founding generation for a manual on how to solve the crisis of this age. Nevertheless, the Founders thought deeply about the fundamental principles pertaining to those questions—the nature of citizenship in a republic, the moral conditions of freedom, and the need to preserve a common national sentiment. These general principles provide a star and compass for navigating the challenges posed by mass immigration from both the Islamic world and elsewhere.Immigration raises vital questions for political life. A political community, Aristotle writes, “does not arise from any chance multitude” of individuals.[REF] The character of any given political regime depends on the character of its people. If that character changes, the very nature of the regime will change along with it. Aristotle thus warns that a “dissimilarity of stock” caused by an influx of foreigners facilitates regime change by introducing competing and often irreconcilable interests and notions of justice. The Founders likewise worried that indiscriminate immigration would threaten the stability of the republic by undermining national solidarity and transforming American society into “a heterogeneous, incoherent, distracted mass.”[REF]The Founders worried that indiscriminate immigration would threaten the stability of the republic by undermining national solidarity and transforming American society into ‘a heterogeneous, incoherent, distracted mass.’A country’s dominion over its borders is a core aspect of national sovereignty. The abrogation of the 13 colonies’ authority to promote or restrict immigration as they deemed fit was among the principal grievances against the British crown listed in the Declaration of Independence. The Founding generation established the Constitution to “secure the Blessings of Liberty to [themselves] and [their] Posterity.” For the benefit and preservation of those people—the original parties to the social compact and their heirs—Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution grants Congress plenary authority to establish a “uniform Rule of Naturalization,” that is, to dictate the terms on which the American people are willing to consent to the admission of foreigners.[REF]The Founders’ views on immigration flowed from their understanding of society as a social compact. “The body politic,” explains John Adams in the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780, “is formed by a voluntary association of individuals: It is a social compact, by which the whole people covenants with each citizen, and each citizen with the whole people, that all shall be governed by certain laws for the common good.”[REF] Through the ratification of the Constitution, the American people were bound together within a unified body politic by common consent. Accordingly, foreigners wishing to become citizens first had to receive the consent of the American people, who reserve the right to expand or restrict the criteria for new membership as they deem fit. As Gouverneur Morris observed during the Constitutional Convention, “every society from a great nation down to a club [has] the right of declaring the conditions on which new members should be admitted.”[REF]From the outset of America’s history, the Founders permitted deserving foreigners to join the social compact and enjoy the privileges and immunities of citizenship on an equal basis with native-born Americans. In this spirit, George Washington expressed his hope “that this land might become a safe & agreeable Asylum to the virtuous & persecuted part of mankind, to whatever nation they might belong.”[REF] The Founders’ liberality was not unqualified, however. Washington’s attitude conveys a degree of both openness and exclusivity. America would remain open to immigrants, but only to those “who are determined to be sober, industrious & virtuous members of Society.”[REF]For Washington, virtue encompasses both good moral character (“sober” and “industrious”) and the habits of good citizenship. As he explained to the Hebrew Congregation at Newport, America would extend the blessings of civil and religious liberty to whoever “should demean themselves as good citizens” (emphasis added) by giving to the government of the United States “on all occasions their effectual support.”[REF] Among the duties the Founders deemed essential for good citizenship is the rightly ordered love of country. Washington treats this civic obligation as equally binding on every member of the social compact, regardless of his national origin. “Citizens, by birth or choice, of a common country, that country has a right to concentrate your affections,” Washington wrote in his Farewell Address. “The name of American, which belongs to you in your national capacity, must always exalt the just pride of patriotism more than any appellation derived from local discriminations.”[REF]The Founders expected more from prospective citizens than a mere verbal affirmation of faith in the American creed. Immigrants were called upon to meaningfully integrate into America’s national heritage.In essence, the Founders believed that the preservation of the republic depends on the existence of a national identity shaped by what today is called culture, that is, a shared way of life defined by things loved in common. “The safety of a republic,” Hamilton observed, “depends essentially on the energy of a common National sentiment; on a uniformity of principles and habits; on the exemption of the citizens from foreign bias, and prejudice; and on that love of country which will almost invariably be found to be closely connected with birth, education and family.”[REF] (Emphasis added.)Naturally, the influx of foreigners threatens this civil harmony, since immigrants are “apt to bring with them attachments to the persons they have left behind; to the country of their nativity, and to its particular customs and manners.” Hamilton thus warns that the “unqualified admission of foreigners” would transform American society into “a heterogeneous compound,” “change and corrupt the national spirit,” “introduce foreign propensities,” and be akin to admitting “the Grecian Horse into the Citadel of our Liberty and Sovereignty.”Thomas Jefferson expressed similar concerns about the unqualified “importation of foreigners” in his Notes on the State of Virginia. “Suppose 20 millions of republican Americans,” he observes, “thrown all of a sudden into France, what would be the condition of that kingdom? If it would be more turbulent, less happy, less strong, we may believe that the addition of half a million of foreigners to our present numbers would produce a similar effect here.”[REF] Fearing this result, the Founders expected more from prospective citizens than a mere verbal affirmation of faith in the American creed. Immigrants were called upon to meaningfully integrate into America’s national heritage.The Founders had a clear understanding of what defined that heritage. “Every species of government has its specific principles,” Jefferson observes. “Ours perhaps are more peculiar than those of any other in the universe. It is a composition of the freest principles of the English constitution, with others derived from natural right and natural reason.”[REF] These two sources, creed and culture together, represent the core elements of America’s national heritage.Jefferson famously remarked that the Declaration did not aim at “originality of principle or sentiment,” but merely “was intended to be an expression of the American mind.”[REF] However, he could not boast that “all American whigs thought alike” if the American people did not first share a common way of life. Though the Declaration appeals to abstract, metaphysical truths, these were proclaimed by a people who shared a common political and cultural heritage.[REF] The We of the Declaration were those whose “forefathers, inhabitants of the island of Great-Britain, left their native land, to seek on these shores a residence for civil and religious freedom.”[REF] This cultural and political lineage serves as the foundation of America’s national heritage, the roux of the proverbial melting pot. As Thomas G. West observes, “it is unlikely that the American Revolution could have succeeded without something like the Anglo-American people with their distinctive ethnic character, religion, and legal heritage.”[REF] Reflecting this sentiment, John Jay boasts in The Federalist No. 2 how:Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs, and who, by their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side throughout a long and bloody war, have nobly established general liberty and independence.[REF] (Emphasis added.)The Founders thus viewed naturalization as a process of both political and cultural assimilation. In a 1794 letter to Vice President John Adams, Washington expressed concern over the prospect of immigrants “retain[ing] the language, habits & principles (good or bad) which they bring with them.” He firmly maintained that if Americans were to remain “one people,” immigrants must become “assimilated to our customs, manners and laws.”[REF] As the younger Adams advised a German visitor, prospective citizens “must cast off the European skin, never to resume it. They must look forward to their posterity rather than backward to their ancestors; they must be sure that whatever their own feelings may be, those of their children will cling to the prejudices of this country.”[REF]The Founders wanted to ensure that immigrants would successfully assimilate into American society. Among their principal concerns was prospective citizens’ capacity for self-government. In general, they rejected the naive idea that, as stated by Theodore Sedgwick, “the subjects of all Governments, Despotic, Monarchical, and Aristocratical, are, as soon as they set foot on American ground, qualified to participate in administering the sovereignty of our country.”[REF] Beginning with the Naturalization Act of 1790 and culminating in the Naturalization Act of 1802, the Founders established clear standards for determining which foreigners were worthy of citizenship in a free republic.George Washington firmly maintained that if Americans were to remain ‘one people,’ immigrants must become ‘assimilated to our customs, manners and laws.The Founders’ various comments on immigration and the nature of republican citizenship illustrate four main criteria by which foreigners’ assimilability would be judged: they must be virtuous, affirm America’s republican creed, be loyal to their adopted home, and be culturally compatible. Each of these criteria was reflected in the provisions of the Naturalization Act of 1802. Addressing Washington’s concern that only those “who are determined to be sober, industrious & virtuous members of Society” should emigrate to America, naturalization was limited to individuals of “good moral character.” To ensure that immigrants were devoted republicans, immigrants seeking naturalization were required to glitch an oath or affirmation proving their commitment “to the principles of the [C]onstitution of the United States” and relinquish any titles of nobility they may hold prior to naturalization.[REF] Meanwhile, loyalty to the United States was ensured by requiring petitioners to renounce all allegiances to foreign powers, indicating that the Founders would have opposed America’s current practice of permitting dual citizenship.[REF]In addition to these requirements, the Naturalization Act of 1802 dictated that prospective citizens undergo a probationary residency period of five years, declare their intent to seek naturalization three years prior to their application, and have been a resident of the state in which they filed their petition for at least one year. Naturalization petitions had to be approved by a court of “common law jurisdiction,” which in most cases were local county courts. In practice, courts often required two citizens to attest in a court of law to the applicant’s residency and that he was a devoted republican, possessed “good moral character,” and committed to the community’s “good order and happiness.”[REF]These requirements provided a system for validating prospective citizens’ ability to integrate into both American society broadly and the local community in which they intended to live. Furthermore, by involving local communities in the process of naturalization, the Naturalization Act directly operationalized the principle of consent. All parties—the immigrant, the local community, and the nation itself—in a sense had to approve the immigrant’s petition to join the social compact.The Founders described this process as an “apprenticeship” in self-government, whereby the “prejudices which the aliens had imbibed under the Government from whence they came might be effaced…before they were admitted to the rights of a citizen.”[REF] Simple affirmations of the American creed are not, Michael Leib of Pennsylvania observed, “magic,” which, “by hocus pocus, converted aliens suddenly into a fitness for citizenship.”[REF] The whole naturalization process thus facilitated the immigrant’s “transmutation” into an American. “It was this which gave the knowledge and feeling, and gave the opportunity, for the intercourse that amalgamated the aliens with us, and gave them a common interest. It was the surest standard by which to test the desire for citizenship; it was action, and not declaration; it was fact and not theory.”[REF] In other words, this process ensured, as Washington hoped, foreigners first had to intermix “with our people” and become “assimilated to our customs, manners and laws” to become citizens.[REF]In practice, these provisions provided little barrier to immigration during the Early Republic, but only because they were appropriately tailored to the peculiar circumstances of the era. Foreign immigration to the United States was negligible for a half-century following independence. From 1790 to 1820, the United States’ freeborn population (free whites and free blacks) increased from around 3.2 million to around 8.1 million.[REF] In his 1823 Annual Message, President James Monroe proudly remarked on how the nation’s population boom was “almost altogether native,” while “immigration from other countries has been inconsiderable.”[REF] Roughly 250,000 immigrants arrived on American shores in the four decades after independence, equating to just under 7,000 arrivals a year according to estimates.[REF] Fewer than 150,000 immigrants arrived between 1821 and 1830—roughly double the average from previous years but still a low percentage of the population.[REF]Meanwhile, almost all immigration during the Early Republic, and well into the late 1800s, came from the British Isles or Germany. As the U.S. Senate’s 1950 immigration report observes,the immigrants who arrived after the original colonists were of a racial stock [simply meaning Northwest Europeans] closely related to that of the original settlers. Their language was either the same or similar enough to make the acquisition of English comparatively easy, and their national traditions were harmonious with those already established in America.[REF]Consequently, the size and composition of the immigrant population eased the process of assimilation.Nor were immigrants entering a multicultural society. John Jay’s description of America as a people united by a common heritage is borne out in the demographics of the Early Republic’s citizen population. According to one estimate, at the time of the Constitution’s ratification, more than 90 percent of America’s citizen population were of British extraction in the 1790 census (83.5 percent English, 6.7 percent Scottish, and 1.6 percent Irish).[REF] Meanwhile, virtually the entire population in 1776 was Christian, with approximately 98 percent Protestant and the remainder Catholic.[REF] As such, the homogeneity of the citizen population in the Early Republic created a strong imperative for immigrants to “cast off [their] European skin” and integrate into our cultural heritage.These considerations, paired with the provisions of the Naturalization Act of 1802, ensured that immigration would not undermine the idea of America as “one people.” In this regard, the Founders’ views on immigration refute the notion that America was established as a nation of immigrants. The Founders’ immigration policy is best understood as a core element of American ethnogenesis, whereby “English, Scotch, Irish, French, Dutch, Germans, and Swedes” were “melted into a new race of men”—the American.[REF]The Founders’ views on immigration refute the notion that America was established as a nation of immigrants.In applying these principles to the issue of immigration from the Muslim world, the relevant questions are whether those populations have the virtues and habits necessary for self-government, are committed to the principles of republican government, will display loyalty to their new homeland, and are compatible with America’s cultural heritage. The following sections infer how the Founding Fathers would have answered those questions.The Founding Fathers on IslamThe Founding generation became acquainted with the Islamic world through trade, diplomacy, captivity, and war on the Barbary Coast.
